title: Radhika Apte
text:
Radhika Apte, born on 7 September 1985 in Vellore, Tamil Nadu, is an Indian actress known for her work in film, television, and theatre. She comes from a Marathi family; her parents were doctors at Christian Medical College & Hospital, Vellore. She earned degrees in Economics and Mathematics from Fergusson College in Pune, where she was homeschooled alongside friends, an experience that boosted her self-confidence. Before entering acting, she trained in Kathak dance for eight years under Rohini Bhate.

Apte's acting career began in theatre, and she made her film debut in 2005 with a small role in *Vaah! Life Ho Toh Aisi!*. Her first lead role came in 2009 with the Bengali drama *Antaheen*, where she played a TV journalist and received praise for her performance. She continued working in Indian regional cinema, appearing in Marathi, Bengali, Tamil, and Telugu films. In 2010, she appeared in *Rakta Charitra* and its sequel, as well as *The Waiting Room*. After a discouraging stint in Mumbai, she moved to London to study contemporary dance, where she met her future husband, musician Benedict Taylor. Upon returning to India, she gradually gained recognition, particularly after her roles in *Badlapur* (2015), *Hunterrr* (2015), and *Manjhi - The Mountain Man* (2015), which earned her critical acclaim.

Her breakout came in 2016 with lead roles in independent films *Phobia* and *Parched*, both of which were well-received. She further cemented her status in 2018 with roles in three Netflix productions: the anthology film *Lust Stories*, the thriller series *Sacred Games*, and the horror mini-series *Ghoul*. Her performance in *Lust Stories* earned her an International Emmy Award nomination, making her the first Indian actress to receive one. She also starred in successful mainstream films like *Kabali* (2016), *Pad Man* (2018), and *Andhadhun* (2018). In 2019, she appeared in the American film *A Call to Spy*, and in 2022, she starred in *Monica, O My Darling*. Her recent work includes the 2024 film *Sister Midnight*, for which she received a British Independent Film Award nomination.

Beyond film, Apte is actively involved in theatre, working with Pune’s Aasakta Kalamanch troupe and performing in plays like *That Time* and *Bombay Black*. She has also appeared in several short films, including *Darmiyan* and *Ahalya*. In 2020, she made her directorial debut with *The Sleepwalkers*, which premiered at the Palm Springs International ShortFest.

Apte has been vocal about sexual harassment in the film industry, supporting the MeToo movement in India. She is known for her unconventional role choices and has been called a "powerhouse performer" and the "poster child of OTT." She endorse brands like Clinique and Sanfe and has been ranked among the best Bollywood actresses by publications like Rediff.com. In 2024, she announced she was pregnant with her first child.

title: Iggy Azalea
text:
Iggy Azalea, born Amethyst Amelia Kelly on 7 June 1990 in Sydney, Australia, is a rapper and songwriter who rose to fame in the United States. Before her music career, Azalea lived in Mullumbimby, raised by her father, a painter and comic artist, and her mother, who worked as a cleaner. Growing up in a hand-built mud-brick house, she began rapping at 14 and briefly formed a group with two other girls, inspired by TLC, before pursuing a solo career. At 16, she moved to the U.S. to pursue music, initially telling her parents she was on a holiday before deciding to stay permanently. She worked in the U.S. illegally for years before obtaining legal status in 2013 and later becoming a permanent resident in 2018.

Azalea gained early recognition with her 2011 mixtape *Ignorant Art* and music videos for "Pussy" and "Two Times" on YouTube. She signed with T.I.'s Grand Hustle Records and released the *Glory* EP in 2012. Her breakout came with her 2014 debut album *The New Classic*, which topped the *Billboard* Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart, making her the first non-American female rapper to achieve this. The album was preceded by hits like "Work" and the chart-topping "Fancy" (featuring Charli XCX), which earned a Grammy nomination. She also appeared on Ariana Grande's "Problem," which peaked at number two, making Azalea one of only two acts (alongside the Beatles) to simultaneously hold the top two spots on the *Billboard* Hot 100 with debut releases. Her other hits included "Black Widow" (featuring Rita Ora) and "Change Your Life" (featuring T.I.).

After *The New Classic*, Azalea faced label disputes and personal struggles, leading to the cancellation of her planned second album, *Digital Distortion*. She switched to Island Records, releasing the *Survive the Summer* EP in 2018. Later, she became an independent artist, launching her own label, Bad Dreams, under Empire. She released *In My Defense* (2019), *Wicked Lips* (2019), and *The End of an Era* (2021). In 2024, she announced her retirement from music.

Azalea has won multiple awards, including two American Music Awards, three Billboard Music Awards, an MTV Video Music Award, a People's Choice Award, and four Teen Choice Awards, along with four Grammy nominations. Her YouTube channel and Vevo videos have garnered billions of views, with 15 of her music videos surpassing 100 million views. Known for her distinct Southern hip-hop influenced style, Azalea remains one of the most successful female rappers in the world.

title: Suthida
text:
Suthida Bajrasudhabimalalakshana, known as Queen Suthida of Thailand, was born Suthida Tidjai on 3 June 1978 in Bangkok. She is the daughter of Kham and Jangheang Tidjai, and she comes from a Thai Chinese family of Hokkien ethnicity. Suthida received her education at Hatyaiwittayalai Somboonkulkanya Middle School and later earned a bachelor’s degree in communication arts from Assumption University in 2000. Before entering royal service, she worked as a flight attendant, first for JALways, a subsidiary of Japan Airlines, from 2000 to 2003, and then for Thai Airways International from 2003 to 2008.

In 2014, Suthida joined the Thai military and was appointed commander of Crown Prince Vajiralongkorn’s household guard. Her rapid rise in the military was notable, as she was promoted to the rank of general by December 2016, just six years after enlisting. During her military career, she completed several training courses and held significant positions, including Commander of the Special Operations Unit of the Royal Security Command. On 1 June 2017, she became the acting commander of the Royal Thai Aide-de-camp Department. Her distinguished service earned her the title *Than Phu Ying* (Dame Grand Cross of the Most Illustrious Order of Chula Chom Klao) in October 2017, making her the first female officer to receive this honor in the reign of King Rama X.

On 1 May 2019, Suthida married King Vajiralongkorn, becoming the fourth queen consort of Thailand. Their wedding took place at the Amphorn Sathan Residential Hall in Bangkok, with Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn and Privy Council President Prem Tinsulanonda as witnesses. The coronation ceremony followed soon after, on 4–6 May 2019. As queen, she has participated in royal duties, including the Royal Ploughing Ceremony in May 2024.

Queen Suthida holds numerous royal honors, including the Most Illustrious Order of the Royal House of Chakri, the Ancient and Auspicious Order of the Nine Gems, and the Most Exalted Order of the White Elephant. She has also been awarded military decorations, such as the Royal Cypher Medals of Kings Rama IX and Rama X, as well as the King Vajiralongkorn’s Court Medal. Her military ranks have progressed from Second Lieutenant in 2010 to General in 2016, with further promotions to Admiral and Air Chief Marshal scheduled for 2025.

Her marriage and royal duties have solidified her position within the Thai monarchy, and she continues to play an active role in ceremonial and official functions alongside the king.

title: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo
text:
Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, born on January 8, 1946, is a notorious Mexican drug kingpin who rose to prominence as the founder and leader of the Guadalajara Cartel in the 1980s. Known by aliases such as "El Jefe de Jefes" (The Boss of Bosses) and "El Padrino" (The Godfather), he played a central role in Mexico’s drug trade, controlling major trafficking routes along the U.S.-Mexico border. His career began after he graduated from college and worked as a bodyguard for the governor of Sinaloa, Leopoldo Sánchez Celis, whose political connections helped him establish his criminal empire. By the early 1980s, Félix Gallardo, along with associates Rafael Caro Quintero and Ernesto Fonseca Carrillo, had taken control of drug trafficking routes after the death of a previous leader, Avilés.

The Guadalajara Cartel became a dominant force in Mexico’s drug trade, particularly after U.S. interdiction efforts in Florida forced Colombian cartels to rely on Mexico as a transshipment hub. Félix Gallardo’s network, which included the future Sinaloa, Tijuana, Juárez, and Pacífico Sur cartels, earned billions by taking a 50% cut of the cocaine they transported. However, his operations faced a major setback in 1985 when DEA agent Enrique "Kiki" Camarena uncovered cartel corruption and destroyed large marijuana plantations. In retaliation, Félix Gallardo allegedly ordered Camarena’s abduction, torture, and murder, which led to a massive DEA investigation, Operation Leyenda. Though Caro Quintero and Carrillo were arrested, Félix Gallardo remained at large due to political protection.

He was finally captured on April 8, 1989, on charges including the murder of Camarena, drug trafficking, and racketeering. His arrest exposed deep corruption within Mexican law enforcement and politics, leading to the dismantling of the Guadalajara Cartel. Before his capture, Félix Gallardo had orchestrated a meeting in Acapulco in 1989, dividing the cartel’s territories among his associates. This decision gave rise to rival cartels, including the Sinaloa Cartel (led by Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán) and the Tijuana Cartel (run by his nephews, the Arellano Félix family).

Félix Gallardo initially received a 40-year sentence, which was extended to 77 years in 2017. Despite his imprisonment, he continued to influence the drug trade from prison using contraband cell phones. His health deteriorated over time, leading to his transfer from a high-security federal prison to a medium-security facility in Guadalajara in 2014. In 2022, he was granted house arrest due to declining health, a decision supported by President López Obrador.

Félix Gallardo’s family has remained deeply involved in the drug trade. His nieces and nephews, including the Arellano Félix brothers, formed the Tijuana Cartel, while his niece Sandra Ávila Beltrán was a key figure in the Sinaloa Cartel. In 2008, portions of his memoirs were published, revealing insights into his life and criminal network. His legacy as a founding figure in Mexico’s drug wars has been depicted in various TV series, including *Narcos: Mexico*, where he was portrayed by Diego Luna. His arrest and the subsequent fragmentation of the Guadalajara Cartel marked the beginning of Mexico’s violent drug wars, which continue to this day.

title: Fernando da Costa Novaes
text:
Fernando da Costa Novaes (April 6, 1927 – March 24, 2004) was a prominent Brazilian ornithologist specializing in the bird fauna of the Amazon region. He dedicated his career to studying and documenting the avian biodiversity of this vast and complex ecosystem, contributing significantly to the understanding of its taxonomic and ecological characteristics. Novaes completed his doctorate in 1971 from the State University of São Paulo at Rio Claro, where his dissertation focused on the ecological study of birds in secondary vegetation areas along the lower Amazon River in Pará, Brazil. This foundational work set the stage for his lifelong research in the region.

Novaes spent much of his professional life at the Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi in Belém, where he curated and expanded the institution's bird collections, making it the second-largest bird skin and skeleton collection in Brazil. The collection was later renamed in his honor, reflecting his enduring contributions to ornithology. His research focused on defining the faunal boundaries and affinities of the Amazon region, as well as resolving taxonomic challenges within the avian species of the area. His work was instrumental in clarifying the distribution and relationships of various bird species, particularly those in the Amazon basin.

In 1954, Novaes received a prestigious Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation fellowship, which allowed him to study at the Museum of Vertebrate Zoology at the University of California, Berkeley, under the renowned ornithologist Alden H. Miller. This experience further refined his expertise and expanded his network in the field of ornithology.

Novaes was a prolific researcher, publishing numerous scientific papers across a wide range of journals. His work covered various aspects of ornithology, including species descriptions, ecological studies, and behavioral observations. Some of his notable publications include studies on the avifauna of the Aripuanã River in Mato Grosso and Amazonas, the Golden Parakeet (*Aratinga guarouba*) in northern Brazil, and the taxonomy of several bird groups, such as the Alagoas foliage-gleaner (*Philydor novaesi*), a species named in his honor. His collaborations with other researchers, such as D.C. Oren and M.F.C. Lima, further enriched his contributions to the field.

Throughout his career, Novaes documented the birdlife of various regions, including the Serra Parima in Roraima, the highlands of the Rio Paru de Leste in Pará, and the Campos de Bragança in Pará. His detailed observations and analyses provided critical insights into the ecological relationships and geographical variations of Amazonian birds. His work also extended to lesser-known or understudied species, helping to fill gaps in the scientific understanding of the region’s avian diversity.

Novaes's legacy in ornithology is marked by his extensive fieldwork, meticulous research, and the establishment of a comprehensive bird collection that continues to serve as a valuable resource for scientists. His contributions to taxonomy, ecology, and conservation have left a lasting impact on the study of Amazonian birds, ensuring that his work remains foundational for future generations of researchers. His name is perpetuated in the scientific community through the species *Philydor novaesi*, a fitting tribute to his dedication to the study of Brazilian birds.

title: Jan Zamoyski
text:
Jan Zamoyski (1542–1605) was one of the most influential Polish noblemen, statesmen, and military leaders of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. Born on March 19, 1542, to Stanisław Zamoyski and Anna Herburt, he was educated in Poland before being sent abroad at 13. He studied in Paris, Strasbourg, and Padua, where he earned a doctorate in law and converted from Calvinism to Catholicism. His early education included political engagement, and in 1563, he became rector of the law department at Padua. He returned to Poland in 1565, receiving a commendation from the Venetian Senate.

Zamoyski quickly rose in political prominence, becoming a key advisor to Kings Sigismund II Augustus and Stephen Báthory. He held multiple high-ranking positions, including Royal Secretary, Deputy Chancellor, Grand Chancellor of the Crown, and Great Hetman of the Crown. He was also General Starost of Kraków and held several other starostwo (administrative districts). As a leader of the *szlachta* (nobility), he championed reforms to strengthen Poland’s parliamentary system, earning the nickname "first tribune of nobility" or "Polish Gracchus."

His political career was marked by both success and controversy. He played a crucial role in the 1573 and 1575 royal elections, opposing Habsburg influence and supporting Báthory’s rise. Despite initial setbacks, such as Henry de Valois abandoning Poland, he regained favor by opposing Habsburg candidates. As Grand Chancellor, he contributed to diplomatic and military efforts, including the war against Muscovy (1579–1581), where he proved himself a capable military leader despite his lack of prior experience. His role in the Siege of Pskov, though inconclusive, drained Russian resources and contributed to the favorable Peace of Yam-Zapolsky.

Zamoyski’s military career peaked during the conflict with Habsburg-backed Maximilian III of Austria in 1588. His victory at the Battle of Byczyna secured Sigismund III Vasa’s claim to the Polish throne. However, his relationship with Sigismund soured over time due to the king’s Habsburg alliances and plans to use Poland for his Swedish ambitions. Zamoyski opposed these policies, leading to a public feud during the Sejm of 1591. Despite tensions, he avoided civil war and later issued a public apology to the king.

Militarily, he led campaigns against Tatar raids and Ottoman influence in Moldavia, achieving victories at Cecora (1595) and Bukova (1600). He also commanded Commonwealth forces in Livonia during the Polish-Swedish War, capturing key strongholds before resigning due to ill health.

Zamoyski was a wealthy magnate, controlling vast estates and founding the Zamoyski Family Fee Tail (ordynacja zamojska), which granted him semi-ducal authority. His most significant cultural legacy was the city of Zamość, designed as a Renaissance "ideal city" by Bernardo Morando. In 1595, he established the Akademia Zamojska, Poland’s third university. He also funded other towns, supported arts and literature, and collected a vast library.

Despite his achievements, Zamoyski’s personality was complex. His conversion to Catholicism was pragmatic, and historians note his occasional greed, such as accepting bribes during negotiations. He died on June 3, 1605, from a stroke, leaving his fortune to his son, Tomasz Zamoyski.

Zamoyski’s legacy endures in Polish historiography and art. He is remembered as a skilled statesman, military leader, and cultural patron, though some critics highlight his flaws. His influence on Poland’s political and military history remains significant, and he is often depicted in paintings, including works by Jan Matejko. Overall, he is considered one of the most prominent figures of the Polish Renaissance, shaping both the Commonwealth’s governance and its cultural development.

title: David Galloway (writer)
text:
David Darryl Galloway (1937–2019) was an accomplished American novelist, curator, journalist, and academic with a multifaceted career that spanned over five decades. Born in Memphis, Tennessee, on May 5, 1937, he attended Harvard University, where he was mentored by notable figures such as Leonard Bernstein and Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr. While at Harvard, he met Radcliffe student Sally Gantt, whom he married in 1959. After their marriage, the couple relocated to the University at Buffalo, where their son was born two years later.

Galloway began his professional life as a publications editor for the Albright-Knox Art Gallery. He later left the United States to teach at Trinity College Dublin and the University of Sussex, simultaneously contributing articles to prominent British newspapers like *The Daily Telegraph*, *The Times*, and *The Guardian*. In 1967, he returned to the U.S. to help establish the New Gallery in Cleveland, which later became the Museum of Contemporary Art Cleveland. In 1972, he moved to Germany, where he was appointed chairman of American Studies at the newly founded Ruhr University Bochum. Around this time, he published his first novel, *Melody Jones*, which received widespread critical praise.

While teaching at Ruhr University, Galloway traveled extensively, lecturing in Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. His connections with the Iran-America Society in Tehran led to a significant opportunity in 1977, when he was hired as the founding curator of the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art. Tasked with assembling a collection to commemorate the tenth anniversary of Empress Farah Pahlavi’s coronation, Galloway curated one of the most important collections of Western art outside the Western world, featuring works by Salvador Dalí, Claude Monet, Pablo Picasso, Vincent van Gogh, and Andy Warhol, alongside Iranian artists like Parviz Tanavoli. However, he left Tehran just months before the Iranian Revolution, returning to Germany to resume his professorship at Ruhr University.

In the 1970s, Galloway also purchased the Maison de Chapitre, the former episcopal residence in Forcalquier, France, which he converted into an informal retreat for artists and students. In 1979, he began contributing to the *International Herald Tribune*, where he maintained close professional relationships with artists such as Pina Bausch, Keith Haring, Yoko Ono, and Andy Warhol. Over the years, he published three more novels: *A Family Album*, *Lamaar Ransom: Private Eye*, and *Tamsen*. After retiring from Ruhr University in 2002, he continued curating exhibitions, including shows at the Venice Biennale and the Moscow Museum of Modern Art, while writing for publications like *Art in America* and *ARTnews*. In 2011, he curated exhibitions of Marilyn Manson’s paintings in Miami Beach and Vienna.

Throughout his career, Galloway contributed to over a hundred books on art, design, literature, and architecture, many of which focused on contemporary artists. Notable works include *Keith Haring* (1992), *The Critical Response to Truman Capote* (1999), and *Marilyn Manson & David Lynch: Genealogies of Pain* (2011). He was also recognized for his scholarly contributions, such as *The Absurd Hero of American Fiction* (1966) and *Henry James: The Portrait of a Lady* (1967). In 1988, he was elected a fellow of the Royal Society of Arts, further cementing his influence in the arts and academia.

Galloway passed away on December 28, 2019, leaving behind a legacy as a prolific writer, influential curator, and dedicated educator who bridged the worlds of academia and contemporary art.

title: John Atkinson Grimshaw
text:
John Atkinson Grimshaw (1836–1893) was a prominent English Victorian artist renowned for his meticulously detailed and atmospheric urban landscapes, particularly his nocturnal scenes. Critics, such as Christopher Wood, praised him as a "remarkable and imaginative painter," and his work was celebrated for its realism and emotional depth. Grimshaw's artistic approach was heavily influenced by photography, a passion of his, and he was known to use tools like the camera obscura to project scenes onto his canvases. This method, though controversial among some contemporaries who saw it as a lack of skill, allowed him to achieve precise detail and lighting effects. His paintings often appeared almost photographic, with critics debating whether they could be considered traditional paintings due to their lack of visible brushwork. Despite this, his mastery of color, light, and shadow, as well as his ability to evoke strong emotions, was widely recognized. The artist James McNeill Whistler, who worked alongside Grimshaw in Chelsea, famously remarked that he had considered himself the inventor of "nocturnes" until he saw Grimshaw's moonlit paintings, highlighting his unique contribution to the genre.

Born in Leeds on 6 September 1836, Grimshaw was the son of Mary and David Grimshaw. In 1856, he married his cousin Frances Hubbard. At the age of 24, he abandoned his clerical job with the Great Northern Railway to pursue painting, much to his parents' dismay. His early works, exhibited in 1862 under the patronage of the Leeds Philosophical and Literary Society, primarily featured birds, fruit, and blossoms. Over time, his artistic style evolved, and he became particularly known for his depictions of moonlit streets and docks in cities like London, Hull, Liverpool, and Glasgow. His ability to capture the mood of urban scenes, particularly under gaslight or twilight, was a defining feature of his work.

By the 1870s, Grimshaw had achieved significant success, allowing him to rent a second home in Scarborough, which became a frequent subject in his paintings. He also moved residences several times, eventually settling in Knostrop Old Hall. In 1890, he and his son Arthur were elected members of the Leeds Photographic Society, reflecting his enduring interest in the medium. Grimshaw died on 31 October 1893 at the age of 57, succumbing to an abscess, and was buried in Woodhouse Cemetery in Leeds. His legacy continued through his artistic descendants, as four of his children—Arthur, Louis, Wilfred, and Elaine—also became painters.

Grimshaw's art was deeply influenced by the Pre-Raphaelites, characterized by its realism, vivid detail, and precise lighting. His paintings often conveyed a sense of warmth and melancholy, capturing the essence of Victorian urban life without dwelling on its harsher realities. Works like *Dulce Domum* (1885) and *On Hampstead Hill* showcase his ability to depict interior scenes and atmospheric cityscapes with remarkable skill. In his later years, he also painted historical and literary subjects, inspired by poets like Longfellow and Tennyson. His urban scenes, particularly those illuminated by twilight or artificial light, were especially popular among his middle-class patrons.

Though Grimshaw left no personal writings, his reputation endured, and his work experienced a resurgence in the late 20th century. Major exhibitions, such as *Atkinson Grimshaw – Painter of Moonlight* (2011), celebrated his contributions to Victorian art. His legacy lies in his ability to transform industrial cityscapes into poetic, dreamlike visions, preserving the beauty and mystery of the Victorian era in his paintings.

title: Richie Dorman
text:
Richie Dorman, born on 14 June 1988 in Hawarden, Wales, is a retired professional footballer who has since transitioned into a career in football administration. He is the brother of fellow footballer Andy Dorman. Dorman began his football journey in the academy of Blackburn Rovers, an English club, before moving to the United States in 2006. There, he played for the New Hampshire Phantoms and also participated in amateur football with the Boston University Terriers. During his early career, Dorman had two stints with Airbus UK, a Welsh club, before moving abroad again in 2011.

In April 2011, Dorman joined Finnish club Kraft on loan, marking the beginning of his time in Finnish football. He later played for SJK (Seinäjoki), where he became a notable player. In June 2014, his performances earned him a spot in the Veikkausliiga 'Team of the Month,' a recognition of his contributions during that period. Dorman’s success continued as he helped SJK win several major trophies, including the Veikkausliiga title in 2015, the Finnish Cup in 2016, and the Finnish League Cup in 2014. Additionally, he was part of the team that won the Ykkönen (the second tier of Finnish football) in 2012, showcasing his role in the club’s rise to the top division.

Following his playing career, Dorman took on a leadership role in football administration. On 30 October 2018, he was appointed as the technical director of SJK Seinäjoki, overseeing the club’s technical aspects. He remained in this position until May 2025, when he left SJK to take up a new role as the sporting director of Burton Albion, an English club competing in League One at the time. This move marked a significant step in his post-playing career, demonstrating his transition from a player to an influential figure in club management.

Throughout his career, Dorman’s contributions to both SJK and Finnish football were significant, earning him recognition and leadership roles. His ability to adapt to different football environments—from English and American clubs to Finnish football—highlighted his versatility and commitment to the sport. As a sporting director, he has continued to impact the game, now focusing on strategic and administrative aspects of football. His journey reflects a well-rounded career that spans playing, coaching, and club management, leaving a lasting legacy in both Welsh and Finnish football.

title: Cheyenne Brando
text:
Tarita Cheyenne Brando, born on 20 February 1970, was a French fashion model and the daughter of legendary actor Marlon Brando. Her mother, Tarita Teriipaia, was an actress from French Polynesia whom Marlon Brando met while filming *Mutiny on the Bounty* in 1962. Cheyenne was born in Tahiti and raised there by her mother after her parents divorced in 1972. Despite her father’s fame, she had a strained relationship with him. Marlon Brando reportedly restricted her and her younger brother, Tehotu, from visiting him in the United States, citing concerns about their Tahitian upbringing making them vulnerable to American culture. As a child, Cheyenne admired her father, but her feelings soured as she grew older. By 1990, she publicly expressed resentment, stating that he had ignored her during her childhood, visiting Tahiti only occasionally and showing little interest in her.

Cheyenne’s teenage years were marked by substance abuse, including LSD, PCP, marijuana, and tranquilizers. She dropped out of high school and began a modeling career, which was cut short in 1989 when she was severely injured in a car crash. The accident occurred after her father refused to let her visit him while he was filming *The Freshman* in Toronto. She suffered a broken jaw, facial lacerations, and a torn ear, requiring extensive reconstructive surgery. The crash left her with lasting physical and emotional scars, leading to depression and a suicide attempt.

In 1987, Cheyenne began a relationship with 23-year-old Dag Drollet, whose father was a prominent figure in French Polynesian politics. The couple became engaged, and in 1989, Cheyenne became pregnant. At Marlon Brando’s request, they moved to his home in Los Angeles to await the birth of their child. Tragedy struck on 16 May 1990, when Cheyenne’s half-brother, Christian Brando, fatally shot Drollet at the house. Christian claimed the shooting was accidental, alleging that Drollet had tried to take a gun from him after Cheyenne accused Drollet of abuse. Christian was arrested and charged with first-degree murder, but prosecutors struggled to prove premeditation without Cheyenne’s testimony. She refused to testify, fled to Tahiti, and gave birth to a son, Tuki Brando, on 26 June 1990. Following the birth, she attempted suicide twice and was hospitalized for drug detoxification. A French judge later declared her "mentally disabled," preventing her from testifying. Christian ultimately pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter and served five years in prison.

The aftermath of the shooting worsened Cheyenne’s mental health. She was diagnosed with schizophrenia, became isolated, and lost custody of Tuki, who was raised by her mother in Tahiti. She made public accusations against her father, claiming he had molested her and was involved in Drollet’s death, though Marlon Brando denied these allegations. Her condition deteriorated further, and on 16 April 1995, at the age of 25, she took her own life by hanging herself at her mother’s home in Tahiti. Neither her father nor her half-brother Christian attended her funeral. She was buried in the Uranie Cemetery in Papeete, alongside Dag Drollet’s family. Tuki Brando later became a model and pursued a career in medicine.

title: Maja Jager
text:
Maja Buskbjerg Jager, born on 22 December 1991 in Nørre Broby, Denmark, is a prominent recurve archer who has represented her country at the highest international levels, including two Olympic Games. She began archery at the age of eight, training in a warehouse in Tilst, arranged by her father, Jan Jager, a fruit grower with local connections. Her early training was overseen by former Danish Olympic archer Ole Gammelgaard. In 2013, Jager moved to Goesan, South Korea, to train under Kim Hyung-Tak, the coach of the 1984 South Korean Olympic archery team, as part of an agreement between Kim and the Danish Archery Federation. To meet South Korean residency requirements, she completed an undergraduate degree in computer system engineering at Jungwon University, despite facing significant challenges adapting to her new environment. She returned to Denmark in 2018 after five years in South Korea and, as of 2019, was pursuing a postgraduate degree at the Technical University of Denmark.

Jager's competitive career began with her debut at the 2009 Archery World Cup, followed by appearances at the 2010 European Archery Championships and the 2011 World Archery Championships, where she finished ninth in the women's individual event. In 2012, she made her Olympic debut at the London Games, competing in the women's team event alongside Carina Christiansen and Louise Laursen. The Danish team set a national record in the ranking round with 1,946 points, advancing to the quarterfinals before being eliminated by South Korea.

In 2013, Jager achieved her most significant success by winning the women's individual title at the World Archery Championships in Belek, Turkey. Entering the tournament with modest expectations, she set a new Danish record in the ranking round with 1,351 points, earning the eighth seed. In a surprising run, she defeated top-ranked archers Ki Bo-bae and Yun Ok-hee before facing Xu Jing in the final. After a tie in the fifth set, Jager won the one-arrow shoot-off by landing her arrow just 1 millimeter closer to the center, securing the championship. She also won a bronze medal in the women's team event with Christiansen and Anne Marie Laursen, marking Denmark's most successful World Championship performance. For her achievements, she was named Danish Sports Name of the Year, an honor shared by the Danish Olympic Committee and *Jyllands-Posten*. Her victory helped popularize archery in Denmark ahead of the 2015 World Championships in Copenhagen.

Jager continued to compete at a high level, winning a silver medal in the mixed team event at the 2014 European Archery Championships with Nikolaj Wulff. The following year, she secured another silver at the European Games, finishing as the runner-up to Germany's Karina Winter in the women's individual event. However, at the 2015 World Championships, she failed to defend her individual title, losing in the second round, and Denmark did not qualify for the team elimination rounds. In 2016, she missed out on Olympic qualification after losing to Carina Christiansen in the qualifying tournament.

At the 2018 European Archery Championships, Jager finished as the runner-up in the women's individual event to Turkey's Yasemin Anagoz in a shoot-off. She later competed at the 2019 European Games, winning a team bronze with Randi Degn and Anne Marie Laursen, but was eliminated in the last sixteen of the individual event. That same year, she qualified for the 2020 Summer Olympics in Tokyo, her second Olympic appearance. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Games were postponed to 2021, where she was eliminated in the second round of the women's individual event by Russia's Ksenia Perova. Throughout her career, Jager has been one of Denmark's most decorated archers, contributing significantly to the sport's growth in her home country.

title: Mihai Eminescu
text:
Mihai Eminescu (1850–1889) is widely regarded as Romania’s most celebrated and influential poet, a central figure of the Romantic movement. Born Mihail Eminovici in Botoșani, Moldavia, his birth date is confirmed as 15 January 1850, though some records list 22 December 1849. His father, Gheorghe Eminovici, was an aristocrat from Bukovina, while his mother, Raluca Iurașcu, came from an old noble family in Hotin. The Eminescu family had roots in Banat, with ancestors migrating to Bukovina in the 18th century. His paternal grandfather, Vasile Iminovici, settled in Călinești, Bukovina, where he worked as a church teacher. Gheorghe Eminovici later became a boyar, serving various noble families, including Alexandru Balș.

Eminescu’s early education took place in Cernăuți (Chernivtsi), where he attended gymnasium and published his first poem, *La mormântul lui Aron Pumnul* (At the Grave of Aron Pumnul), in 1866. His literary career began with contributions to *Familia* magazine, where he adopted the pen name "Mihai Eminescu." In 1869, he co-founded the *Orient* literary circle, focusing on Romanian folklore, and briefly worked as a clerk for theatrical troupes in Bucharest. That same year, he embarked on studies in Vienna, though without formal university admission, attending lectures as an auditor. He befriended the Junimea literary society, whose leaders, including Titu Maiorescu and Iacob Negruzzi, would shape his career.

In Vienna, Eminescu continued writing and publishing, including his notable poem *Venus și Madonă* (Venus and Madonna). He later studied in Berlin (1872–1874) on a Junimea stipend. From 1874 to 1877, he worked in Iași as the director of the Central Library, a school inspector, and editor of *Curierul de Iași*. He befriended writer Ion Creangă, encouraging him to join Junimea. Moving to Bucharest in 1877, he became editor-in-chief of *Timpul* (The Time), the Conservative Party’s newspaper, where he wrote influential editorials during Romania’s war with the Ottoman Empire and the 1878 Treaty of Berlin. He opposed clauses granting citizenship to Jews and ceding southern Bessarabia to Russia.

Eminescu’s major works include *Luceafărul*, *Odă în metru antic* (Ode in Ancient Meter), and the satirical *Scrisorile* (Letters). His poetry often explored metaphysical, mythological, and historical themes, earning him recognition as a linguistic innovator. His manuscripts, totaling 46 volumes and 14,000 pages, were donated to the Romanian Academy in 1902.

His later years were marked by deteriorating health. In 1883, he suffered a nervous breakdown and was treated for alleged syphilis, though modern research suggests this diagnosis was incorrect. He received mercury treatments, which likely contributed to his decline. Hospitalized in Bucharest, he died on 15 June 1889 at the Caritas Institute. His death remains debated, with theories ranging from mercury poisoning to a head injury inflicted by another patient. His brain was lost during autopsy, complicating investigations.

Eminescu’s legacy is immense. Historians like Nicolae Iorga credit him with shaping modern Romanian language and literature, akin to Shakespeare’s influence on English. His works remain foundational in Romanian culture, and he is often celebrated as the national poet. His life, though cut short, left an indelible mark on Romanian literature and identity.

title: Amr Shabana
text:
Amr Shabana, born on 20 July 1979 in Cairo, Egypt, is a retired professional squash player widely regarded as one of the greatest in the sport's history. Known for his left-handed play, Shabana began making a name for himself early in his career, reaching the final of the British Under-14 Open in 1993 and the British Under-19 Open in 1997, though he lost both times to compatriot Ahmed Faizy. He became a member of the Professional Squash Association (PSA) in 1995 and quickly established himself as a rising star, winning his first two tour titles in July 1999—the Puebla Open and the Mexico Open—both against Australia’s Craig Rowland.

Shabana’s breakthrough came in 2003 when, as the ninth seed, he won the World Open, squash’s premier tournament. He defeated top players like David Palmer, Anthony Ricketts, and Karim Darwish before claiming the title by beating Thierry Lincou in the final. This victory made him the first Egyptian to win the World Open. Despite a sluggish 2004, where his only notable final was a loss to Palmer in the British Open, Shabana rebounded in 2005 with the help of a new coach, manager, and personal life changes. He won multiple titles, including the St. Louis Open and the Hungarian Open, before securing his second World Open title in Hong Kong, defeating Palmer in the final.

His dominance continued into 2006, with victories in the Canadian Classic, the Tournament of Champions in New York, and the Bermuda PSA Masters, increasing his PSA Tour title count to 12. In April 2006, he became the first Egyptian to reach the World No. 1 ranking. In 2007, he won his third World Open, solidifying his status as an elite player. His reign as World No. 1 lasted 33 months before being surpassed by fellow Egyptian Karim Darwish in January 2009.

Shabana’s later career included notable achievements, such as becoming the oldest professional to win a World Series title in 2014 by defeating Grégory Gaultier in the Tournament of Champions. Over his career, he won four World Open titles (2003, 2005, 2007, 2009) and reached numerous other major finals, including the British Open, Hong Kong Open, Qatar Classic, and US Open. He also played a key role in Egypt’s success in international team competitions, notably the 1999 and 2009 Men’s World Team Squash Championships.

Shabana retired from professional squash on 27 August 2015, leaving behind a legacy marked by 30 PSA titles and a reputation as one of the sport’s finest players. His career was defined by consistency, resilience, and a remarkable ability to perform at the highest level, earning him a place among the all-time greats of squash.

title: Sage Stallone
text:
Sage Moonblood Stallone, born on May 5, 1976, in Los Angeles, California, was an American actor and the eldest child of actor Sylvester Stallone. His mother was Sasha Czack, and he had one brother, Seargeoh "Seth" Stallone, as well as three half-siblings: Sophia, Sistine, and Scarlet Stallone. His extended family included his uncle, actor and singer Frank Stallone, and his grandmother, Jackie Stallone, who was known for her involvement in wrestling promotions. Later in life, he became the stepson of Jennifer Flavin, Sylvester Stallone’s wife. Sage attended Montclair College Preparatory School in Van Nuys, California, graduating in 1993, and briefly studied filmmaking at the University of North Carolina School of the Arts.

Stallone’s acting career began in his childhood with a guest appearance on *Gorgeous Ladies of Wrestling*, a show promoted by his grandmother. His first major acting role came in *Rocky V* (1990), where he played Robert Balboa Jr., the son of his father’s iconic character, Rocky Balboa. He later appeared alongside Sylvester Stallone in *Daylight* (1996). Beyond these roles, he worked in low-budget exploitation films. In 1996, he co-founded Grindhouse Releasing with film editor Bob Murawski, a company dedicated to restoring and preserving exploitation films, including titles like *Cannibal Holocaust* and *Gone with the Pope*.

In 2006, Stallone directed his first film, *Vic*, which he also wrote and produced. The movie earned him the "Best New Filmmaker" award at the Boston Film Festival. He did not reprise his *Rocky* role in *Rocky Balboa* (2006) because he was focused on his own project. Later, he appeared in Vincent Gallo’s films *Promises Written in Water* and *The Agent*, both of which premiered at major film festivals, including the Venice Film Festival and the Toronto International Film Festival. A photograph of him as a young boy with his father appeared in *Creed* (2015), where it was mentioned that his character had moved to Vancouver.

Tragically, Sage Stallone was found dead on July 13, 2012, at his home in Studio City, Los Angeles, at the age of 36. Reports indicated that he had not been heard from for four days before his death. An autopsy and toxicology tests revealed that he died from coronary artery disease caused by atherosclerosis, with no illegal drugs detected, though hydrocodone, prescribed after a dental procedure, was present. At the time of his death, he was reportedly engaged. His funeral took place on July 21 at St. Martin of Tours Catholic Church in Los Angeles, and he was buried at Westwood Village Memorial Park Cemetery.

title: Braulio Lara
text:
Braulio Armando Lara Peguero was a Dominican professional baseball pitcher born on December 20, 1988, and died tragically in a car crash on April 20, 2019. His career spanned multiple teams across minor league baseball, a brief stint in the Korean Baseball Organization (KBO), and a short period in the Mexican Baseball League. Lara began his professional career in 2008 when he signed as an international free agent with the Tampa Bay Rays. His first two seasons were spent with the Dominican Summer League Rays, where he compiled a 7–5 record and a 3.73 ERA in 30 appearances. After being released in late 2009, he re-signed with the Rays in 2010 and played for the rookie-level Princeton Rays, achieving a 6–4 record and a 2.18 ERA with 58 strikeouts in 13 starts.

In 2011, Lara advanced to Single-A with the Bowling Green Hot Rods, starting 25 games and posting a 5–11 record with a 4.94 ERA and 111 strikeouts in 120+1⁄3 innings. The following year, he pitched for the High-A Charlotte Stone Crabs, where his performance declined slightly with a 6–10 record, a 5.71 ERA, and 82 strikeouts in 112 innings. On December 6, 2012, the Miami Marlins selected Lara in the Rule 5 draft, but he was returned to the Rays just over three months later. In 2013, he split time between Double-A Montgomery Biscuits and made his Triple-A debut with the Durham Bulls, finishing the season with a 4.38 ERA in 72 innings across 45 games. The 2014 season saw him continue between Montgomery and Durham, though his ERA rose to 5.77 in 57+2⁄3 innings.

In November 2014, Lara signed a minor league deal with the San Francisco Giants, including an invitation to spring training. He spent 2015 between Double-A Richmond and Triple-A Sacramento, recording a 6.08 ERA in 32 games. The following year, he began with Sacramento again, posting a 3.90 ERA in 27+2⁄3 innings before signing with the SK Wyverns of the KBO League on June 23, 2016. However, his time in Korea was unsuccessful, as he went 2–6 with a 6.70 ERA in 17 games (9 starts) and 48+1⁄3 innings.

After returning to the United States, Lara signed with the Washington Nationals in November 2016 and spent the 2017 season with their Double-A affiliate, the Harrisburg Senators, where he had a 4.08 ERA in 34 appearances. Following the season, he declared free agency. In 2018, Lara joined the Sultanes de Monterrey in the Mexican Baseball League, appearing in 17 games with a 5.23 ERA. Later that year, he was traded to the Generales de Durango but was released after just two games due to poor performance. Lara’s career came to an abrupt end when he died in a car accident in the Dominican Republic on April 20, 2019, at the age of 30. His professional journey included stops in multiple organizations and leagues, though he never reached the major leagues.

title: Katherine Ryan
text:
Katherine Louisa Ryan, born in June 1983, is a Canadian comedian, writer, presenter, actress, and singer who has made a significant impact in British entertainment. She was raised in Sarnia, Ontario, by her Irish-Canadian father, Finbar, a draughtsman, and her mother, Julie McCarthy, who runs an IT consulting company. Ryan has two younger sisters, and her parents separated when she was a teenager. She studied city planning at Ryerson University (now Toronto Metropolitan University) in Toronto, where she worked at Hooters and began performing at open mic nights, developing a comedy routine. She also appeared as a dancer in MuchMusic's *Electric Circus*.

After graduation, Ryan worked as a corporate trainer for Hooters, eventually moving to the UK in 2007 to open a branch in Nottingham. She quickly established herself in British comedy, winning the Funny Women Award in 2008. Her early TV appearances included *Video on Trial* in Canada and *Campus* in the UK. She gained further recognition as a panelist on shows like *8 Out of 10 Cats*, *Never Mind the Buzzcocks*, *A League of Their Own*, *Mock the Week*, *Would I Lie to You?*, and *QI*. In 2015, she took over as host of *Hair* on BBC Two.

Ryan's stand-up career flourished with two Netflix specials: *Katherine Ryan: In Trouble* (2017) and *Katherine Ryan: Glitter Room* (2019). She also embarked on a successful comedy tour, *Kathbum*, named after a childhood nickname. Beyond comedy, she has acted in sitcoms like *Episodes*, *Badults*, and her own Netflix show *The Duchess*, which she wrote, produced, and starred in. She has also appeared in *Murdoch Mysteries* and voiced a character in the animated series *Counterfeit Cat*.

Ryan has hosted or appeared on numerous TV shows, including *Taskmaster* (which she won in 2016), *Your Face or Mine?*, *The Fix*, *All That Glitters: Britain's Next Jewellery Star*, and *Ready to Mingle*. In 2021, she appeared on *The Masked Singer* as "Pigeon," and in 2025, she was announced as a judge for *Canada's Got Talent* and the reunion host of *The Real Housewives of London*.

Her career has not been without controversy. In 2013, she faced backlash for a joke on *Mock the Week* about Filipino children, leading to protests. She was also accused of racism for a comment about Boris Johnson during an interview, though the BBC defended her as part of her comedic style. In 2023, she won the Outstanding Female Comedy Entertainment Performance award at the National Comedy Awards.

In her personal life, Ryan has been open about her health, having been diagnosed with stage II melanoma in her twenties and another early melanoma in 2025. She had a daughter at age 25 and later entered a civil partnership with Bobby Kootstra in 2019, reuniting with her teenage sweetheart after meeting again while filming *Who Do You Think You Are?*. They have two children together, with a fourth child expected in 2025. Ryan has also been in a relationship with American comedian Alex Edelman.

title: Matthew Perry
text:
Matthew Langford Perry, born on August 19, 1969, in Williamstown, Massachusetts, was an American and Canadian actor, comedian, director, and screenwriter best known for his role as Chandler Bing on the beloved NBC sitcom *Friends* (1994–2004). His performance earned him a Primetime Emmy Award nomination in 2002. Perry's career spanned television and film, with notable roles in *The West Wing* (2003), *The Ron Clark Story* (2006), and *Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip* (2006–2007). He also starred in films such as *Fools Rush In* (1997), *Three to Tango* (1999), *The Whole Nine Yards* (2000), and *17 Again* (2009). Additionally, he co-created and starred in *Mr. Sunshine* (2011) and *The Odd Couple* (2015–2017), and made appearances in *The Good Wife* and *The Good Fight*. His final television role was in *Friends: The Reunion* (2021).

Perry's early life was marked by instability; his parents separated when he was a year old, and he was raised primarily by his Canadian mother, journalist Suzanne Morrison, in Ottawa. He attended boarding school and struggled with feelings of isolation, leading to early rebellious behavior. At 14, he began drinking heavily, and by 18, he was a daily drinker. Despite excelling at tennis as a youth, he shifted focus to acting after moving to Los Angeles at 15. He studied at the Buckley School and took improv classes, landing early roles in TV shows like *Second Chance* and *Growing Pains*.

His breakthrough came with *Friends*, which became a global phenomenon. Perry’s portrayal of the sarcastic, neurotic Chandler made him a household name, though his personal struggles with addiction began to overshadow his success. He battled substance abuse for decades, becoming addicted to alcohol, Vicodin, and other drugs. In 2001, he entered rehab, and in 2018, he nearly died from a gastrointestinal perforation caused by opioid abuse, spending two weeks in a coma. Despite multiple rehab stints and near-fatal health crises, Perry became an advocate for addiction recovery, founding Perry House, a rehab facility, and receiving the Champion of Recovery Award in 2013.

In 2022, he published his memoir, *Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing*, which detailed his lifelong struggle with addiction. The book became a bestseller, and proceeds supported addiction recovery efforts. Perry was engaged to Molly Hurwitz in 2020, but the relationship ended the following year.

On October 28, 2023, Perry was found unresponsive in a hot tub at his Pacific Palisades home and pronounced dead at age 54. An autopsy revealed his death was caused by accidental drowning due to the acute effects of ketamine, with contributing factors including buprenorphine, drowning, and coronary artery disease. Five individuals faced legal charges for supplying him with lethal doses of the drug. His funeral was attended by family and *Friends* co-stars, and the National Philanthropic Trust established the Matthew Perry Foundation in his honor to support addiction recovery initiatives.

title: Abdulqawi Yusuf
text:
Abdulqawi Ahmed Yusuf is a prominent Somali lawyer and judge who has made significant contributions to international law. Born in Eyl, a town in the northeastern region of Puntland, Somalia, he obtained his Juris Doctor from the Somali National University and later earned a PhD in international law from the Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva. Prior to his doctorate, he pursued post-graduate studies in international law at the University of Florence, Italy. Yusuf is multilingual, fluent in Somali, Arabic, English, French, and Italian.

Yusuf’s career has been marked by a series of high-profile roles in international organizations and academia. From 1974 to 1981, he served as a lecturer in law at the Somali National University, and later, from 1981 to 1983, at the University of Geneva. He also represented Somalia as a delegate to the Third United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea between 1975 and 1980. Throughout his career, he has held significant positions at various United Nations bodies, including as Legal Adviser and Director of the Office of International Standards and Legal Affairs at UNESCO from 2001 to 2009, Legal Advisor at UNIDO in Vienna, and Representative of the New York office of UNCTAD. Additionally, he served as Chief of the Legal Policies Service at UNCTAD from 1987 to 1992. His academic contributions extend to serving as a guest professor and lecturer at universities in Switzerland, Italy, Greece, and France.

Yusuf has been an influential figure in international legal institutions. In 1999, he was elected to the Institut de droit international, and he remains an active member. He is the founder and General Editor of the *African Yearbook of International Law* and a co-founder of the African Foundation for International Law, where he also serves as chairperson of its executive committee. His scholarly work includes numerous books and articles on international law, as well as op-eds on Northeast African and Somali affairs. He is a member of the editorial advisory board of the *Asian Yearbook of International Law* and the curatorium of the Thessaloniki Institute of Public International Law and International Relations.

In 2009, Yusuf was appointed as a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), where he served until 2025. During his tenure, he held several key positions, including Vice-President from 2015 to 2018 and President from 2018 to 2021, making him the third African to lead the court after Nigeria’s Taslim Olawale Elias and Algeria’s Mohamed Bedjaoui. In 2011, he also joined the advisory council of The Hague Institute for Global Justice. Yusuf announced his resignation from the ICJ in 2025, effective from September 30 of that year, with the UN Security Council and General Assembly set to elect a successor to complete his term, which would have ended in February 2027.

Yusuf’s extensive publication record includes notable works such as *Panafricanisme et droit international* (2017), *Intellectual Property and International Trade: The TRIPS Agreement* (co-edited with C. Correa, 2016), and *Pan-Africanism and International Law* (2014). He has also edited volumes on the African Union’s legal framework and UNESCO’s standard-setting processes. His early work, *Legal Aspects of Trade Preferences for Developing States* (1982), reflects his long-standing interest in the intersection of international law and development. Through his academic, judicial, and institutional roles, Yusuf has shaped the field of international law, particularly in relation to African and global governance.

title: Heinrich Himmler
text:
Heinrich Himmler (1900–1945) was a central figure in Nazi Germany, serving as the Reichsführer-SS (leader of the Schutzstaffel, or SS) and a key architect of the Holocaust. Born into a middle-class Catholic family in Munich, Himmler struggled with health issues in his youth but developed a strong interest in German nationalism, antisemitism, and occult beliefs. He joined the Nazi Party in 1923 and became involved in the Beer Hall Putsch, though he was not charged for his role. After abandoning Catholicism, he became deeply invested in Nazi ideology, particularly its racial theories and antisemitic policies.

Himmler rose rapidly within the SS, becoming its leader in 1929. Under his command, the SS grew from a small bodyguard unit into a powerful paramilitary organization, separate from the larger Sturmabteilung (SA). He implemented strict racial criteria for SS membership, ensuring members were of "Aryan" descent, and established the SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA) to enforce these policies. He also appointed trusted subordinates like Reinhard Heydrich, who became a key figure in Nazi intelligence and repression.

As the Nazi Party gained power in the early 1930s, Himmler and the SS played a crucial role in consolidating Hitler’s dictatorship. After the Reichstag Fire (1933), Himmler expanded his influence by taking control of state police forces, particularly the political police, which later became the Gestapo. He worked closely with Hermann Göring and Wilhelm Frick to centralize police powers under Nazi control. By 1934, the SS had replaced the SA as the dominant paramilitary force, and Himmler’s authority grew significantly.

Himmler was a driving force behind Nazi racial policies, including the persecution and extermination of Jews, Roma, and other groups deemed undesirable. He oversaw the establishment of concentration and extermination camps, as well as the Einsatzgruppen, mobile killing squads that murdered millions during the Holocaust. In 1941, he commissioned the Generalplan Ost, a blueprint for the conquest and depopulation of Eastern Europe, which resulted in mass killings and forced resettlement.

During World War II, Himmler held various military and administrative positions, including command of the Waffen-SS, a combat branch of the SS. However, his military leadership was largely ineffective, and he was removed from key commands in 1945. As Germany faced defeat, Himmler attempted to negotiate a separate peace with the Western Allies, but Hitler discovered the betrayal and dismissed him. Captured by British forces, Himmler committed suicide on May 23, 1945, avoiding trial for his role in Nazi atrocities.

Himmler’s legacy is one of unparalleled brutality, as he was directly responsible for the systematic murder of millions and the institutionalization of genocide. His organization of the SS into a disciplined, ideological force ensured its role as the enforcer of Nazi racial and political policies. His death marked the end of a man whose actions had devastating consequences for Europe and the world.

title: Namita Gokhale
text:
Namita Gokhale, born in 1956 in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, is a multifaceted figure in Indian literature, known as a novelist, editor, festival director, and publisher. Her literary career began in 1984 with the release of her debut novel, *Paro: Dreams of Passion*, a work that captured the social satire of Delhi’s elite with sharp humor and boldness. The novel, which revolved around the lives of the wealthy and famous in Bombay and Delhi, was initially met with controversy in India but was later recognized internationally as a work of literary fiction. *Paro* became a cult classic and was reissued alongside its 2011 sequel, *Priya: In Incredible Indyaa*, though the latter received a more mixed reception.

Gokhale’s early life was shaped by her upbringing in Nainital, where she was raised by her aunts and grandmother. She studied English literature at Delhi University’s Jesus and Mary College but left at 26 after refusing a course on Geoffrey Chaucer. By 40, she had survived cancer and experienced the loss of her husband, Rajiv Gokhale, whom she married at 18. Despite these challenges, she built a prolific career in writing and publishing.

Beyond fiction, Gokhale has contributed significantly to nonfiction, editing anthologies and writing on Indian mythology, philosophy, and regional culture. Her 1994 work, *Mountain Echoes: Reminiscences of Kumaoni Women*, is an oral biography exploring the lives of Kumaoni women, including her grandmother and aunts. Another notable work, *The Book of Shiva* (2000), delves into Shaivaite philosophy, reflecting her deep fascination with Indian mythology. She also co-edited *The Puffin Mahabharata* (2009), an illustrated adaptation for children, and *In Search of Sita* (2009), a collection of essays on the goddess Sita.

Gokhale’s most acclaimed novel, *Things to Leave Behind* (2016), won the 2021 Sahitya Akademi Award. The novel, part of a trilogy set in the Kumaon hills, explores themes of patriarchy, women’s struggles, and regional history. Critics praised its vivid portrayal of the Himalayan landscape and its nuanced portrayal of societal constraints. Her other notable works include *Lost in Time* (2017), a young adult novel blending time travel and mythology, and *Jaipur Journals* (2020), which captures the essence of the Jaipur Literature Festival.

In addition to writing, Gokhale has been instrumental in promoting literature through initiatives like the Jaipur Literature Festival, which she co-founded with William Dalrymple and Sanjoy K Roy. She also conceptualized and hosted *Kitaabnama: Books and Beyond*, a multilingual book show on Doordarshan that highlighted India’s literary diversity. She co-founded Yatra Books, a multilingual publishing house specializing in translations and creative writing.

Gokhale’s influences range from classical literature to regional folklore, with authors like Tolstoy, Dostoyevsky, and Muriel Spark shaping her literary style. Her works often reflect her Kumaoni Brahmin heritage, as well as her deep connection to the Himalayas. She has received numerous accolades, including the Valley of Words Book Award, the Sushila Devi Literature Award, and the 7th Yamin Hazarika Woman of Substance Award, solidifying her place as a key figure in contemporary Indian literature.

title: Muhammad Al-Hafiz
text:
Muhammad Al-Hafiz, born Hamzah on 15 March 1984, is a former Malaysian professional footballer who played as a goalkeeper. He began his football career in the youth system of Kedah FA, specifically in their President Cup team, and progressed through the ranks. His first appearance in the senior squad came in 2004, when he replaced Megat Amir Faisal Al Khalidi Ibrahim as the backup goalkeeper. That year, the Malaysia Super League was introduced, and Al-Hafiz was initially a second-choice goalkeeper behind Megat Amir Faisal. However, he got his big break in the first league match of the season on 14 February 2004, when Megat Amir Faisal suffered a serious back injury during pre-season preparations, allowing Al-Hafiz to make his senior debut against Selangor Public Bank FC.

Al-Hafiz remained with Kedah FA for several years, developing his skills and gaining experience as a professional goalkeeper. In 2012, he moved to USM FC, which was then competing in the Malaysia Premier League. His time at USM FC was relatively short, as the club faced financial difficulties and withdrew from the league after just one season. This led Al-Hafiz to join Johor Darul Takzim FC in 2013, a club known for its star-studded squad. Despite a mixed start to the season, Al-Hafiz quickly established himself as the first-choice goalkeeper and held that position throughout the campaign.

During his time with Johor Darul Takzim FC, Al-Hafiz contributed to several notable achievements. In 2014, he helped the team win the Malaysia Super League, followed by another league title in 2015. The club also secured the Malaysian Charity Shield in 2015. Additionally, Al-Hafiz was part of the team that reached the final of the 2014 Malaysia Cup, though they finished as runners-up. They also reached the final of the 2013 Malaysia FA Cup but were again unsuccessful in securing the trophy.

Al-Hafiz's career highlights include his consistency and reliability as a goalkeeper, particularly during his tenure at Johor Darul Takzim FC. His ability to secure a starting position in a competitive team and contribute to multiple championship wins underscores his skill and professionalism.
