title: Jan-Michael Gambill
text:
Jan-Michael Gambill, born on June 3, 1977, was an American professional tennis player who turned pro in 1996. He achieved a career-high singles ranking of world No. 14 on June 18, 2001, and was best known for his distinctive double-handed forehand. During his career, he reached the quarterfinals of the 2000 Wimbledon Championships and the final of the 2001 Miami Masters, as well as winning three ATP singles titles. Gambill began playing tennis at the age of five, inspired by legends like Jimmy Connors and John McEnroe. Throughout his career, he defeated numerous top players, including former world No. 1s such as Roger Federer, Carlos Moyá, Lleyton Hewitt, Gustavo Kuerten, Marcelo Ríos, Jim Courier, Pete Sampras, and Andre Agassi, as well as Grand Slam champions like Michael Chang, Thomas Johansson, Sergi Bruguera, and Gastón Gaudio.

His most notable Grand Slam performance came in 2000 at Wimbledon, where he defeated Lleyton Hewitt, Fabrice Santoro, Paul Goldstein, and Thomas Enqvist before losing to eventual champion Pete Sampras in the quarterfinals. The following year, he reached the final of the Miami Masters, defeating Hewitt, Gaudio, and Enqvist along the way. Gambill was coached by his father, Chuck Gambill, who also coached his younger brother, Torrey, another professional tennis player. Despite his success, Gambill’s career was plagued by injuries, particularly a recurring shin condition that limited his play after 2004. He also developed a shoulder injury due to serving harder to compensate for reduced mobility.

After 2005, Gambill’s professional playing career waned, though he continued to compete at lower levels. From 2008 onward, he played for the Boston Lobsters in the World Team Tennis league, alongside former top players like Andre Agassi, John Isner, and Robby Ginepri. In 2009, he reached the semifinals of a Futures tournament in the U.S., and in 2010, he competed in three Challenger events before stepping away from professional competition in October of that year. Since 2011, he has transitioned into coaching, working with top players such as CoCo Vandeweghe, whom he coached on the WTA Tour, and Jared Donaldson, whom he coached on the ATP Tour. As of 2020, Gambill has also worked as a sports analyst for the Tennis Channel.

Beyond tennis, Gambill has been involved in philanthropy, supporting organizations like Cat Tales Zoological Park, which rescues big cats, and Elton John’s AIDS Foundation. He was sponsored by Jaguar and Prince for racquets and apparel. Gambill currently resides in both Los Angeles and Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, with his partner, Malek Alqadi, an architect and developer. He has been open about his personal life, identifying as gay and maintaining a public relationship with Alqadi. Gambill’s career highlights include three ATP singles titles and victories over some of the biggest names in tennis, but injuries and health issues ultimately cut short what could have been a more successful career. His post-playing career has focused on coaching and broadcasting, allowing him to remain involved in the sport he has loved since childhood.

title: Henryk Wieniawski
text:
Henryk Wieniawski (1835–1880) was a Polish virtuoso violinist, composer, and pedagogue widely regarded as one of the greatest violinists in history. Born in Lublin, Poland, his father, Tadeusz Wieniawski, had Jewish roots and had converted to Catholicism before marrying Henryk’s mother, Regina Wolff. Wieniawski’s prodigious talent was evident early in his life, and at just eight years old, he was admitted to the Paris Conservatoire, where he studied under Lambert Massart from 1843 to 1846 and again in 1849.

After graduating, Wieniawski embarked on extensive tours, often accompanied by his younger brother Józef, a pianist. His first composition, *Grand Caprice Fantastique* (Op. 1), was published in 1847, marking the beginning of a prolific output that included 24 opus numbers. His touring career was punctuated by notable events, such as the composition of *Légende* (Op. 17), which he wrote to persuade the parents of his fiancée, Isabella Hampton, to approve their marriage. The couple wed in 1860. Wieniawski also performed as a violist in the Beethoven Quartet Society in London.

In 1860, he moved to St. Petersburg at the invitation of Anton Rubinstein, where he taught violin, led the Russian Musical Society’s orchestra, and performed in its string quartet. From 1872 to 1874, he toured the United States with Rubinstein. In 1875, he succeeded Henri Vieuxtemps as a professor at the Conservatoire Royal de Bruxelles, though his health soon declined. He frequently had to pause during concerts, and in 1879, he embarked on a tour of Russia but was hospitalized in Odessa after a performance. His condition worsened, and he died of a heart attack in Moscow on March 31, 1880. He was buried in Warsaw’s Powązki Cemetery.

Wieniawski’s legacy as a composer is significant, particularly in the violin repertoire. His two most famous works, the *Violin Concerto No. 1 in F-sharp minor* (Op. 14, 1853) and the *Violin Concerto No. 2 in D minor* (Op. 22, 1862), remain central to the violinist’s repertoire, with the second concerto being more frequently performed. His *L'École moderne: 10 Études-Caprices* (Op. 10) is also highly regarded, often placed just below Paganini’s caprices in technical difficulty. Other notable works include *Légende*, *Polonaise Brillante No. 1* (Op. 4), and *Scherzo-Tarantelle* (Op. 16).

Wieniawski’s influence extended to pedagogy, particularly his strict bowing technique, sometimes called the "Wieniawski bow hold" or "Russian bow hold," which allowed him to execute a rapid, controlled staccato known as the "devil’s staccato." This technique was used to refine students' playing.

Posthumously, Wieniawski received numerous honors, including his portrait on Polish postage stamps in 1952 and 1957, and a 100-złoty coin in 1979. The first violin competition named after him was held in 1935, with Ginette Neveu winning first prize. The International Henryk Wieniawski Violin Competition has been held every five years since 1952.

Wieniawski’s musical lineage continued through his daughters. Régine, born in 1879, became a composer, publishing early works under the name Irène Wieniawska before adopting the pseudonym "Poldowski" after marrying into British nobility. Another daughter, Henriette, married Joseph Holland Loring, a victim of the *Titanic* disaster in 1912.

Wieniawski’s contributions as a performer, composer, and teacher solidified his place among the most distinguished violinists of the 19th century, leaving an enduring impact on classical music.

title: Josh Mansour
text:
Joshua Mansour, born on 17 June 1990 in Sydney, Australia, is a former professional rugby league footballer who played primarily as a winger. He represented both Lebanon and Australia at the international level and had a distinguished career in the National Rugby League (NRL), playing for the Penrith Panthers, South Sydney Rabbitohs, and Newtown Jets. Mansour is of Lebanese and Cuban descent through his father, Fidel, who was born near Beirut, and Portuguese descent through his mother, Angie, who hails from the Madeira archipelago.

Mansour began his rugby league journey playing junior football for the St Johns Eagles and Kingsgrove Colts before attending Holy Spirit College in Lakemba. His professional career started with the South Sydney Rabbitohs, where he played in their NYC team from 2008 to 2010. He earned recognition as the NYC Player of the Year and Winger of the Year in 2010. That same year, he represented Lebanon in the European Cup and the Junior Kangaroos. After strong performances in the NSW Cup with the North Sydney Bears, Mansour caught the attention of the Penrith Panthers, who signed him for the 2012 season.

Mansour made his NRL debut for Penrith in 2012, scoring a try on debut and finishing his rookie season with seven tries in 14 games. He re-signed with the club in 2013 and 2014, becoming the Panthers' highest try-scorer in 2014 with 15 tries. That year, he also debuted for the Australian national team in the Four Nations tournament, playing in the final against New Zealand. In 2015, he was named in Lebanon’s World Cup qualifiers squad but did not play.

A standout moment in his career came in 2016 when he played for NSW City Origin and was selected for the NSW State of Origin team, featuring in all three matches. He won the Dally M Winger of the Year award that season and played in the 2016 Four Nations, though a knee injury sustained in a freak training accident sidelined him for much of 2017. He returned in June 2017 and played his 100th NRL game later that year. Mansour was part of Australia’s 2017 World Cup-winning squad, though he did not play in the final.

In 2018, Mansour suffered a severe facial injury after being kneed in the face during a match. After recovering, he signed a three-year extension with Penrith. However, his form declined in 2019, leading to a brief demotion to reserve grade before being recalled. In 2020, he played a key role as Penrith reached the NRL Grand Final, scoring a try in the loss to Melbourne. Following the season, he was informed he would not be required for 2021 and subsequently signed with the South Sydney Rabbitohs.

At South Sydney, Mansour had a strong start in 2021, scoring multiple tries in several matches before a knee injury ended his season. He played sporadically in 2022 before being released. He briefly joined Newtown in 2023 before retiring later that year.

Mansour also represented Lebanon in the 2021 World Cup, scoring a hat-trick in a group-stage match. In his personal life, he is married with two children and is a fan of Arsenal F.C. He co-founded the podcast and YouTube show *Let’s Trot Show*. After his retirement, Mansour publicly criticized South Sydney’s head coach, Jason Demetriou, citing a lack of rapport and dishonesty in their professional relationship.

title: Kubota Beisen
text:
Kubota Beisen (1852–1906) was a significant Japanese artist and art educator during the Meiji period, known for blending traditional Japanese techniques with Western artistic principles. Though he received formal training under Suzuki Hyakunen, his integration of Western perspective and methods was largely self-taught. This fusion of styles allowed him to create works that remained distinctly Japanese while incorporating modern influences. Kubota played a key role in the establishment of the Kyoto Prefectural School of Painting in 1878, alongside other prominent artists such as Kōno Bairei, contributing to the development of art education in Japan.

Throughout his career, Kubota gained recognition for his contributions to both official and commercial projects. In 1886, he was commissioned to decorate the ceiling and doors of a newly constructed room in the Imperial Palace in Tokyo. His international reputation grew after a visit to Paris in 1889, where he studied European masters, and he received a Gold Medal at the Paris Exposition that same year. His work was also celebrated at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago, where he earned a First Class Medal. The Kokumin Shimbun, a major newspaper, employed him as an artist, and his illustrations were widely disseminated to Japanese audiences.

Kubota’s career was marked by his work as a war artist during the First Sino-Japanese War (1894–1895). Assigned by the Kokumin Shimbun, he documented battlefield scenes, providing vivid portrayals of Japan’s military campaigns. His illustrations were compiled into a series of books, *Nisshin Sentou Gahou* (A Pictorial Record of the Sino-Japanese War), which chronicled key events from the outbreak of hostilities to the signing of the peace treaty. His wartime depictions were so highly regarded that he was summoned to General Headquarters to create drawings in the presence of the Emperor. Additionally, his work was included among the gifts presented to Queen Victoria during her Diamond Jubilee in 1897, further solidifying his international standing.

Kubota’s published works include a mix of artistic and theoretical writings, such as *The New Theory of Aesthetics* (1905) and *Beisen gadan* (1901), as well as his wartime illustrations, *Sino-Japanese Campaign at the Front* (1895). His contributions to Japanese art were extensive, with his works held in numerous libraries and institutions worldwide. His legacy endures in both his artistic production and his role as an educator, shaping the trajectory of Japanese art during a period of rapid modernization.

title: Tracy Somerset, Duchess of Beaufort
text:
Tracy Louise Somerset, Duchess of Beaufort (née Ward), born on 22 December 1958 in Kensington, is a British duchess, environmental activist, and former actress. She is often known by her married name, Tracy Worcester, which she frequently used before 2017, and was credited as Tracy-Louise Ward during her acting career. She was previously married to the 12th Duke of Beaufort, Henry Somerset, whom she divorced in 2018. Before her marriage, she worked as a model in Paris, at Christie’s auction house in London, and in art galleries in New York. In her early twenties, she trained as an actress at the Academy of Live and Recorded Arts and the London Drama School. Her most notable acting roles include Tessa Robinson in the television series *C.A.T.S. Eyes* (1986–1987), appearances in *Dance with a Stranger* (1985) and *Timelash* (a *Doctor Who* serial from 1985), and portraying the first Miss Scarlett in the game show *Cluedo* (1990). She also performed in theatre productions such as *Our Day Out* and *Intimacy*.

Tracy comes from a notable aristocratic background. Her father, the Hon. Peter Alistair Ward, was a younger son of the 3rd Earl of Dudley and became chairman of the family business, Baggeridge Brick. Her mother, Clare Leonora Baring, was the daughter of the cricketer Giles Baring. Tracy’s sister is the actress Rachel Ward, and she has one full brother and two half-brothers from her father’s second marriage. Her great-grandfather, the 2nd Earl of Dudley, served as Lord Lieutenant of Ireland and later as Governor-General of Australia, overseeing extensive landholdings, coal and iron mines, and steelworks in Staffordshire and Worcestershire. Tracy grew up on her father’s estate at Cornwell, Oxfordshire.

She married Henry, Marquess of Worcester (later the 12th Duke of Beaufort), on 13 June 1987, in a wedding attended by the then Prince and Princess of Wales (Charles III and Diana). The couple had three children, including Henry Robert FitzRoy Somerset, Marquess of Worcester. They divorced in 2018, shortly after Henry inherited the dukedom.

Since 1989, Tracy has been an active environmentalist, beginning her advocacy with Friends of the Earth. She has held positions with organizations such as The Gaia Foundation, the International Society for Ecology and Culture, the Schumacher Society, the Bath Environment Centre, the Soil Association, and the International Forum on Globalisation. A vocal critic of the European Union, she was a member of the Referendum Party, which opposed British involvement in the bloc. Her environmental work focuses on promoting local food economies, and she has directed documentaries like *Is Small Still Beautiful in India* and *The Politics of Happiness in Bhutan*. In 2009, her documentary *Pig Business* aired on Channel 4, exposing the harmful effects of intensive factory pig farming.

Through her campaigning organization Farms Not Factories, she advocates for high-welfare, locally sourced meat and encourages consumers to avoid factory-farmed products. She has engaged in high-profile stunts with celebrities like Jerome Flynn and Dominic West to raise awareness about factory farming and has collaborated with chefs such as Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall and Mark Hix. As part of her activism, she has purchased shares in major food retailers like Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Domino’s, and Greggs to lobby against their use of factory-farmed pork. She has also conducted undercover investigations into UK pig farms.

Politically, she endorsed Green Party candidate Caroline Lucas in the 2015 general election and campaigned for Jeremy Corbyn in 2019. She now supports George Galloway’s Workers Party of Britain. In 2012, she was one of nine people to provide bail sureties for Wikileaks founder Julian Assange. In 2020, she launched Forbidden Fruit and Veg, a chemical-free organic market garden at her Badminton estate, employing WWOOF (World Wide Opportunities on Organic Farms) participants. She also publishes a monthly newsletter.

Tracy Worcester’s work spans multiple fields, from acting and aristocracy to environmental activism, demonstrating a lifelong commitment to social and ecological causes.

title: Carlos P. Romulo
text:
Carlos P. Romulo Sr. (1899–1985) was a distinguished Filipino statesman, diplomat, soldier, journalist, and author who played a significant role in Philippine and international politics. Born in Intramuros, Manila, to Pangasinense parents, Romulo's father initially fought against the U.S. in the Philippine-American War but later became a government official. Romulo himself began his career as a professor of English at the University of the Philippines and as a secretary to Senate President Manuel Quezon. In the 1930s, he became a publisher and editor of *The Philippines Herald* and co-founded the Boy Scouts of the Philippines.

During World War II, Romulo served as an aide to General Douglas MacArthur and later became a member of President Quezon’s War Cabinet, rising to the rank of general. He was a vocal advocate for Philippine independence, framing American colonialism favorably compared to European rule. After the war, he served as the Philippines’ resident commissioner to the U.S. Congress, becoming the only U.S. congressional member to leave office due to his country’s independence.

Romulo’s diplomatic career spanned eight Philippine presidencies, from Quezon to Marcos, including roles as secretary of foreign affairs, secretary of education, and ambassador to the United States. A key figure at the United Nations, he was elected president of the General Assembly in 1949, the first Asian to hold the position, and chaired the Security Council four times. He was known for his strong stance on human rights and decolonization, famously rebuking a Soviet official who dismissed him as a "little man from a little country" with a defiant response about "little Davids" standing against "blustering Goliaths."

At the 1947 UN vote on the Palestine partition plan, Romulo initially opposed the proposal but was recalled after U.S. pressure led to a change in the Philippines’ stance. He ran for UN secretary-general in 1953 but lost to Lester B. Pearson. A staunch anti-communist, Romulo emphasized the threats of communism in Asia, though his views were often unpopular at the 1955 Bandung Conference.

Romulo briefly pursued Philippine politics, running for the Liberal Party’s presidential nomination in 1953 but losing to Elpidio Quirino. He later managed Ramón Magsaysay’s successful campaign. He served as foreign secretary under Presidents Quirino, Macapagal, and Marcos, resigning in 1983 after the assassination of Benigno Aquino, citing health and moral concerns over Marcos’ regime.

A prolific writer, Romulo authored 22 books, including war memoirs and his autobiography, *I Walked with Heroes*. He was named a National Artist for Literature and received numerous honors, including the Pulitzer Prize, the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and 72 honorary degrees. He died in 1985 and was buried at the Libingan ng mga Bayani. His legacy endures as a champion of internationalism, democracy, and Philippine sovereignty.

title: Arthur Ewert
text:
Arthur Ernest Ewert was a German communist activist and high-ranking official in the Communist International (Comintern), born on November 30, 1890, in Heinrichswalde, East Prussia (now Slavsk, Russia). He came from a poor peasant family and received only a primary school education. At 14, he moved to Berlin to work as an apprentice in a saddle-making factory but later switched to a steel plant, where his experiences radicalized him. Influenced by his socialist activist sister, Minna, and his future partner, Elise Saborovsky (known as "Szabo"), Ewert joined the Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD) in 1908.

In 1914, Ewert and Szabo moved to Canada, where they evaded internment during World War I by going underground. They joined the Socialist Party of North America (SPNA) and adopted aliases to avoid detection. After being arrested in 1919 for their political activities, Ewert was deported to Germany, while Szabo was interned and later deported. They reunited in Berlin in 1919 and joined the newly formed Communist Party of Germany (KPD). Ewert became a leading KPD activist at the AEG electrical corporation and participated in revolutionary efforts, including violent clashes with nationalist groups.

The Comintern, under Soviet direction, heavily funded the KPD in hopes of a German revolution to support the Soviet cause. Ewert was involved in the failed March Action uprising in 1921, which led to his arrest and brief imprisonment. Despite the KPD's setbacks, Ewert rose through the party ranks, serving on the National Committee (Zentrale) and Politburo. He was also a delegate to multiple Comintern gatherings, where he chaired discussions on British and American communist movements.

By 1928, Ewert was a top KPD leader, serving in the Reichstag and later becoming the KPD's representative to the Comintern. However, his political career faltered when he was labeled a "Conciliator" for opposing the Comintern's radical "Third Period" policies. After public self-criticism, he was removed from leadership and reassigned to Latin America.

Ewert was sent to Argentina in 1930 to work with Comintern representative August Guralsky. Their mission was to recruit the influential Brazilian leader Luís Carlos Prestes into the Communist Party of Brazil (PCB), which they successfully accomplished. Later, Ewert and Szabo were dispatched to China as Comintern representatives to the Chinese Communist Party (1932–1934). In 1935, they returned to Brazil, where Ewert was arrested after a failed communist insurrection. He and Szabo were brutally tortured, but neither betrayed their comrades. Szabo was deported to Nazi Germany, where she died in 1939. Ewert, driven insane by his torture, was sentenced to 13 years in prison.

In 1945, Ewert was granted amnesty and returned to East Germany in 1947. However, his mental health never recovered, and he spent the rest of his life in a sanatorium. He died on July 3, 1959, in Ebertswalde. In 1981, the East German government issued a postage stamp in his honor.

title: Matt Hunter (singer)
text:
Matt Hunter, born Matthew Alexander Hunter Correa on February 20, 1998, in New York City, is an American singer, songwriter, and voice actor with Colombian-Italian heritage. Raised in Paramus, New Jersey, he began his career in voice acting at the age of nine, portraying the character Diego Márquez in the final two seasons of Nickelodeon’s *Go, Diego, Go!* and its sister series *Dora the Explorer*. He voiced the role from 2008 to 2010, shortly before transitioning into music.

Hunter’s musical career started when he uploaded YouTube videos of himself playing the guitar and singing covers in both English and Spanish. His videos gained significant attention, leading to a grassroots fanbase across Latin America. By the age of 13, he had released his debut single, “Mi Amor,” followed by “Right Here, Right Now” and “Mi Señorita” in 2012. His early success earned him comparisons to Justin Bieber, with Latin music legend Marc Anthony calling him “the future” of the industry. In 2013, he released his first EP, *Right Here, Right Now*, further establishing his presence in the music world. The following year, he collaborated with Pitbull on two World Cup-themed tracks, “Minha Mina Ta Loca” and “Mi Chica Está Loca,” which were released in both Portuguese and Spanish versions.

By 2016, Hunter had amassed over 200,000 subscribers on YouTube and 500,000 followers on Twitter. His discography expanded with numerous singles, including “Te Necesito” (featuring Augusto Schuster), “Dicen” (a duet with Lele Pons), and “Cazador” (with Lenny Tavarez), showcasing his versatility in both English and Spanish music. He also recorded covers, such as John Legend’s “All of Me” and a Spanish rendition of Justin Timberlake’s “Not a Bad Thing” titled “Todo Cambiará.”

Hunter’s live performances have taken him across the United States, Latin America, and Europe, including sold-out shows in major venues like Chile’s 12,000-seat Movistar Arena in 2013. His appeal spans multiple genres, blending pop, Latin, and urban influences. Beyond music, he produced a weekly comedy web series called *Fuego Fridays* and was nominated for Favorite Pop Artist at the 2013 Premios Juventud, further solidifying his status as a rising star in both English and Spanish-speaking markets.

As of 2020, Hunter continued to release new music, including collaborations with artists like Corina Smith, Carla Fernandes, and Lalo Ebratt. His ability to navigate between languages and genres, along with his early rise to fame, has cemented his place as a notable figure in contemporary Latin and pop music. He splits his time between New York, Los Angeles, Miami, and various Latin American countries, maintaining a strong connection with his diverse fanbase.

title: Flavio Méndez Santiago
text:
Flavio Méndez Santiago, known by his alias *El Amarillo*, was a prominent Mexican drug lord affiliated with Los Zetas, one of the country’s most violent and powerful cartels. His criminal activities drew significant attention from international authorities, particularly the United States, due to his role in drug trafficking operations.

In March 2010, Méndez Santiago was sanctioned by the U.S. Department of the Treasury under the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act, commonly referred to as the "Kingpin Act." This designation was part of a broader action targeting fifty-three other individuals and ten foreign entities involved in drug trafficking. The sanctions effectively prohibited U.S. citizens and businesses from engaging in any financial or commercial transactions with him, and any of his assets within the United States were frozen. The Kingpin Act is designed to disrupt the financial networks of major drug traffickers, making it difficult for them to operate both domestically and internationally.

Despite the sanctions, Méndez Santiago remained active in Los Zetas’ operations. However, his involvement in the cartel eventually led to his arrest. On January 18, 2011, Mexican authorities captured him in Villa de Etla, a municipality in the state of Oaxaca. His arrest was a notable success in the ongoing efforts to dismantle Los Zetas and other drug trafficking organizations that have long plagued Mexico.

The article also notes that Méndez Santiago was listed among Mexico’s 37 most-wanted drug lords, underscoring his significance within the cartel and the broader narcotics trade. His capture was a key moment in the fight against organized crime, though the influence of Los Zetas and other cartels has persisted in Mexico despite such high-profile arrests. The article provides a concise overview of his criminal career, his designation as a kingpin, and his eventual detention, highlighting the challenges of combating drug trafficking in the region.

title: Ivan Toms
text:
Ivan Peter Toms (1952–2008) was a South African physician, anti-Apartheid activist, and advocate for marginalized communities. Born in Johannesburg on 11 July 1952, he attended Glenwood High School in Durban, where he was Deputy Head Prefect and captain of the second rugby team. He later studied medicine at the University of Cape Town (UCT), receiving his MB ChB in 1976. While at UCT, he participated in a protest against the Bantu Education system, during which he was beaten by police and suffered a broken nose. After graduation, he interned at Kimberley Hospital and later earned a BA in theology.

Toms was drafted into the South African Defence Force (SADF) in 1978 as a non-combatant doctor. He served six months in Namibia, then under South African control, but opposed the SADF’s mission. Upon returning to Cape Town, he was asked by the South African Christian Leadership Assembly to establish a medical clinic in the Crossroads squatter settlement, where he became the sole doctor for 60,000 residents. In 1983, he witnessed violent police raids on Crossroads, which led him to publicly oppose the SADF and co-found the End Conscription Campaign (ECC) alongside activists like Nan Cross. The ECC sought to resist compulsory military service, which Toms viewed as deeply unjust. In 1985, he went on a three-week hunger strike to protest the government’s demolition of Crossroads, during which he declared his refusal to serve in the SADF again. The clinic was later taken over by the SADF, and in 1987, Toms defied a conscription order, leading to his 1988 imprisonment for nine months in Pollsmoor Prison.

Toms was also a prominent gay rights activist, co-founding Lesbians and Gays Against Oppression (LAGO) in 1987. His advocacy for LGBTQ+ rights made him a target of homophobic attacks. After Apartheid ended in 1991, he became national coordinator of the National Progressive Primary Healthcare Network, focusing on health programs in informal settlements and pioneering AIDS advocacy, including the use of antiretroviral drugs. In 1993, he led the Students' Health and Welfare Centres Organisation, which provided mobile medical services in poor areas. By 1996, he was appointed Health Director for the City of Cape Town, later becoming executive director in 2002. His legacy includes the Ivan Toms Centre for Men’s Health in Greenpoint, Cape Town, which focuses on sexually transmitted infections. In 2006, President Thabo Mbeki honored him with the bronze Order of the Baobab for his contributions to social justice and public health.

Toms died suddenly from meningococcal meningitis on 25 March 2008, at age 55. His death was widely mourned, with tributes from figures like Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who praised his selflessness and commitment to equality. His funeral, attended by hundreds, was held at St. George’s Cathedral in Cape Town. Toms remains remembered for his unwavering dedication to human rights, healthcare, and social justice in South Africa.

title: John Morris (curler)
text:
John Morris, born December 16, 1978, in Gloucester, Ontario (now part of Ottawa), is a highly decorated Canadian curler and two-time Olympic gold medallist. Nicknamed "Johnny Mo," he is the son of Maureen and Earle Morris, the inventor of the "Stabilizer" curling broom. Morris began curling at the age of five at the Navy Curling Club. He is also the author of the book *Fit to Curl*.

Morris achieved significant success as a junior curler, skipping his Ottawa Curling Club team to three consecutive Ontario provincial junior men's titles from 1997 to 1999. He won the Canadian and World Junior Championships in 1998 and 1999, setting records with his victories. His junior team, which included Craig Savill, Matt St. Louis, and Mark Homan, later evolved with players like Andy Ormsby and Brent Laing. In 1999, he also won a provincial junior mixed title with Jacqueline Smith, Brent Laing, and Chrissy Cadorin.

After his junior career, Morris moved to Southwestern Ontario to attend Wilfrid Laurier University and curled out of the Stayner Granite Club. His team, which included Savill, Jason Young, and Andy Ormsby, had early success, winning tour events and qualifying for the 2001 Ontario Nokia Cup, where they lost in the final. In 2002, they won the Ontario provincial championship, earning Morris a spot at the 2002 Nokia Brier, where they finished as runners-up to Alberta's Randy Ferbey. The following year, they reached the finals of the inaugural Canada Cup, also losing to Ferbey. After moving to Calgary in 2003, Morris formed a new team with Kevin Koe, Marc Kennedy, and Paul Moffatt, winning the 2004 Players' Championship Grand Slam.

In 2006, Morris joined forces with veteran skip Kevin Martin, forming a team with a four-year plan aimed at winning Olympic gold. They won the 2007 provincial championship and the 2007 Tim Hortons Brier, where Morris was named all-star third despite being injured. The team dominated the Grand Slam circuit, winning three of four events in their first season. Despite injuries, including a broken hand at the 2008 Brier, they won the 2008 and 2009 Briers, as well as the 2009 World Men's Curling Championship. They also won the 2010 Olympic gold medal, defeating Norway in the final. The team continued to excel, winning multiple Grand Slams and the 2011 Canada Cup. However, they struggled at the 2012 Alberta provincials and the 2013 Brier before parting ways in April 2013.

Morris then joined Jim Cotter's British Columbia team, winning the 2014 provincial championship and finishing as Brier runners-up. In 2015, he skipped Team Canada at the Brier, leading them to victory and a bronze medal at the World Championships. After a disappointing 2016 Brier, he returned to Cotter's team, winning the 2017 provincials and the 2017 Elite 10 Grand Slam. At the 2017 Olympic Trials, Morris and Cotter struggled, but in 2018, Morris teamed up with Kaitlyn Lawes to win the mixed doubles Olympic Trials and the gold medal at the 2018 Winter Olympics.

After the Olympics, Morris focused on mixed doubles, competing with multiple partners and winning several events. In 2020, he joined Kevin Koe's team as their second, competing at the 2020 Brier as an alternate. His career has been marked by versatility, leadership, and consistent high-level performance across multiple provinces and disciplines.

title: Salome Maswime
text:
Salome Maswime is a prominent South African clinician and global health expert specializing in obstetrics and gynecology. She currently serves as the Head of Global Surgery at the University of Cape Town, where she advocates for women's health rights, equitable access to surgical and maternal care, and improved healthcare services for remote and underserved populations. Her work extends beyond clinical practice, as she consults for organizations like the World Health Organization (WHO), providing expertise on critical health issues. In 2017, she received the Trailblazer and Young Achiever Award, and she is also a member of the Academy of Science of South Africa, highlighting her significant contributions to the field.

Born in Limpopo, Maswime initially pursued medicine at the University of KwaZulu-Natal, graduating in 2005. During her medical internship, she witnessed two maternal deaths in a maternity ward in Greytown, KwaZulu-Natal, an experience that deeply impacted her and drove her to specialize in obstetrics and gynecology. She feared becoming part of a system that allowed preventable maternal deaths, a concern that shaped her career. After completing her medical degree, she spent a decade at the University of the Witwatersrand and the Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital in Soweto. During this time, she recognized the need to address the underlying causes of poor maternal and neonatal outcomes, leading her to pursue further education.

Supported by the Carnegie Corporation of New York and the South African Medical Research Council, Maswime completed her Master's and PhD at the University of the Witwatersrand. Her research focused on reducing maternal morbidity from cesarean section-related hemorrhage across 15 hospitals in Gauteng, demonstrating her commitment to improving surgical outcomes. She later became an executive member of the South African Perioperative Research Group and a member of the International Network of Obstetric Survey Systems, further solidifying her role as a leader in maternal health research.

Maswime’s work has revealed alarming statistics, such as Africa accounting for 200,000 maternal deaths annually—two-thirds of global maternal deaths. In 2017, she was recognized by the *Mail & Guardian* as one of the Top 200 South Africans for her contributions. She has also authored articles in *The Conversation* on the increasing number of cesarean sections in Africa. In 2018, she founded the South African Clinician Scientists Society, an organization dedicated to mentorship, networking, and research collaboration among emerging specialists. That same year, she received a prestigious Discovery Foundation Harvard University and Massachusetts General Hospital Fellowship, worth R2.1 million, to study the causes of stillbirths in HIV-positive individuals. Her research also explores the mental health of mothers and children, reflecting her holistic approach to women’s health.

In 2019, Maswime was appointed Professor of Global Surgery at the University of Cape Town, expanding her influence in the field. In 2020, she was named one of the World Economic Forum’s Class of 2020 Young Scientists, a distinction recognizing her as one of 25 researchers at the forefront of scientific discovery. Despite her demanding career, she balances her professional life with family, raising two children, Taurai (12) and Farai (8). Throughout her journey, Maswime has been a trailblazer, advocating for systemic change in maternal and surgical care while inspiring the next generation of clinicians and researchers.

title: Karni Liddell
text:
Karni Liddell, born on 1 March 1979 in Rockhampton, Queensland, is an Australian Paralympic swimmer and radio presenter. Her life has been marked by both athletic achievement and personal medical challenges. At just twelve months old, she was diagnosed with Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a rare neuromuscular disease. For over four decades, this diagnosis stood, but in 2019, after a lengthy and expensive search for answers, she underwent a whole genome sequencing test in Europe that revealed she actually had Congenital Titinopathy, another neuromuscular wasting disease. Her family had spent twelve years seeking a proper diagnosis, and the misdiagnosis proved traumatic. Doctors initially told her parents she would never walk and would not survive past her teenage years, but she defied those predictions.

Beyond her medical struggles, Liddell has been a prominent figure in Australian disability sports. By the age of 14, she had already broken a world record in swimming. She competed in two Paralympic Games—Atlanta in 1996 and Sydney in 2000—winning medals at both. Notably, she served as the captain of the Australian Swimming Team at the 2000 Sydney Paralympics. Her leadership and dedication to the sport made her a standout figure in Paralympic swimming.

Liddell’s influence extends beyond the pool. In 2004, she was one of eighteen Australian Paralympians featured in a nude calendar photographed by Emma Hack. For her photo, she wore sunglasses and body paint designed to resemble a polka-dotted bikini, showcasing her strength and confidence. Additionally, in 2008, her image was painted by artist Ludmila Clark, and the artwork was displayed at the Customs House in Rockhampton, further cementing her place in the public eye.

Currently, Liddell works as a radio presenter for 4BC, continuing to engage with the public and inspire others. Her journey—marked by perseverance in the face of medical uncertainty, athletic excellence, and public advocacy—makes her a notable figure in both sports and disability awareness.

title: Tappaya Sit-Or
text:
Tappaya Sit-Or, also known as Mit Klinmee, is a retired Muay Thai legend born on February 1, 1976, in Thailand. As a former Rajadamnern and WMC champion, he was a dominant force in the sport, particularly in the 1990s, before transitioning into coaching. Tappaya came from a fighting family, being the youngest of 11 children and beginning his training at just 6 years old alongside his brother, Yokthai Sit-Or, and nephew, Rambaa Somdet. The trio trained relentlessly before and after school and even competed in local bars for tips in their early years. By 12, Tappaya was already fighting professionally in Bangkok, establishing himself as a rising star.

His career reached its peak in 1997 when he defeated Ankandet BaoBaoin to win the 61.5 kg Rajadamnern title, a belt he held for three consecutive years. That same year, he also claimed the WMC lightweight championship by beating Panmongkon Carryboy. Despite being ranked first at Lumpini Stadium, he did not win a title there, though his prominence grew as he became a regular on Channel 7, one of Thailand’s major sports broadcasters. His career record stands at an impressive 200 wins, 36 losses, and five draws, solidifying his legacy as one of the sport’s greatest fighters.

In the later stages of his career, Tappaya expanded his fighting repertoire by traveling to China, Japan, and the United Kingdom, where he competed in Muay Thai, kickboxing, and even mixed martial arts. While in Japan, he fought under the Crosspoint Gym banner and secured a notable victory over Hayato in a kickboxing match. After retiring from competition in 2001, he pursued his long-held ambition of opening his own gym, which he accomplished in 2009. Today, he runs the Sor Klinmee Gym in Pattaya, where he serves as the head trainer.

The gym has produced several notable fighters, including Robert Sor Klinmee, a southpaw competing at 46 kg at Rajadamnern, and Sangpet Sor Klinmee, an orthodox fighter active at both Rajadamnern and Lumpini. Prominent fighters such as Sinsamut and Sudsakorn Sor Klinmee, as well as Yokthai’s son, Thepprasit champion Fasai Sor Klinmee, also train at the gym. Tappaya’s influence extends to a roster of younger fighters who continue the legacy of the Sit-Or and Klinmee camps.

Beyond his fighting and coaching career, Tappaya’s achievements include holding the 1997 Rajadamnern Stadium Lightweight (135 lbs) title and the 1997 WMC World Lightweight Championship. His contributions to Muay Thai, both as a competitor and a mentor, have left an enduring mark on the sport.

title: Ronaldinho
text:
Ronaldinho Gaúcho, born Ronaldo de Assis Moreira on 21 March 1980 in Porto Alegre, Brazil, is widely regarded as one of the greatest footballers of all time. Nicknamed "O Bruxo" (The Wizard), he played as an attacking midfielder or left winger, known for his dribbling, free-kick accuracy, and creative play. He won two FIFA World Player of the Year awards and a Ballon d'Or, and is the only player to have won a World Cup, Copa América, Confederations Cup, Champions League, Copa Libertadores, and Ballon d'Or. His career spanned top clubs in Brazil, Europe, and Mexico, and he remains a global football icon.

Ronaldinho began his career with Grêmio in 1998, where he quickly became a star, scoring 22 goals in his breakout season. In 2001, he moved to Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) in France, winning the UEFA Intertoto Cup. Despite initial success, his time at PSG was marred by off-field distractions, and he transferred to Barcelona in 2003 for €30 million. His time at Barcelona marked the peak of his career. In the 2004–05 season, he won La Liga and was named FIFA World Player of the Year. The following season, 2005–06, was arguably his best, as he led Barcelona to a historic double—winning both La Liga and the UEFA Champions League. His performances in El Clásico, including a 3–0 victory over Real Madrid where he received a standing ovation from Madrid fans, cemented his legend. He won the Ballon d'Or and a second FIFA World Player of the Year award that year.

After Barcelona, Ronaldinho’s form declined, and he joined AC Milan in 2008, winning Serie A in 2011. He returned to Brazil, playing for Flamengo and Atlético Mineiro, where he won the 2013 Copa Libertadores. Later, he had stints in Mexico with Querétaro and briefly with Fluminense in 2015 before retiring.

With the Brazilian national team, Ronaldinho earned 97 caps and scored 33 goals. He was part of Brazil’s 2002 FIFA World Cup-winning team, forming a legendary attack with Ronaldo and Rivaldo. He also captained Brazil to the 2005 Confederations Cup victory and led the Olympic team to a bronze medal in 2008.

Ronaldinho’s early life was marked by tragedy when his father drowned when he was eight. His older brother, Roberto, managed his career, while his sister, Deisi, worked as his press coordinator. His football skills developed in futsal and beach football, which influenced his signature moves. At 13, he scored all 23 goals in a match, drawing media attention.

Throughout his career, Ronaldinho received numerous accolades, including being named in the FIFA 100 list of the world’s greatest living players by Pelé in 2004. In 2009, he was voted World Player of the Decade, ahead of Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo. His legacy endures as one of football’s most talented and entertaining players.

title: Rana Sanaullah
text:
Rana Sanaullah Khan, born on January 1, 1955, is a Pakistani lawyer and politician who has held significant positions in both provincial and federal governments. Currently, he serves as the Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs, a role he assumed in April 2024. Before this, he was the 39th Interior Minister of Pakistan under Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's government. He is widely regarded as the second most influential official in the current administration. Additionally, he is a senior leader of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and has been the party’s president in Punjab since May 4, 2019.

Sanaullah’s political career spans several decades, beginning with his election to the Provincial Assembly of Punjab as a candidate of the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) in 1990. He later switched allegiance to the PML-N and was re-elected to the provincial assembly multiple times in 1997, 2002, 2008, and 2013. During his time in the Punjab Assembly, he held key ministerial positions, including Law and Parliamentary Affairs Minister, Local Governments and Community Development Minister, and Revenue Minister. He also served as the Deputy Leader of the Opposition in the Punjab Assembly during two separate periods—from 1990 to 1993 and from 2002 to 2007.

In 2018, he was elected to the National Assembly of Pakistan, representing Faisalabad, and continued in this role until 2023. Despite running in the 2024 general election as a PML-N candidate, he lost to independent candidate Dr. Nisar Ahmed Jutt. His tenure as Interior Minister began in April 2022 following the ousting of Imran Khan’s government.

Sanaullah’s political career has been marred by controversies. In 2010, as Punjab’s Law Minister, he was accused of having ties with militant organizations, particularly the Sipah-e-Sahaba Pakistan (SSP), a group known for targeting religious minorities. He met with SSP leader Maulana Ahmed Ludhianvi, justifying the alliance on electoral grounds. Additionally, in 2011, he falsely accused American contractor Warren Weinstein of being a spy, leading to Weinstein’s eventual death in a U.S. drone strike.

One of the most contentious incidents involving Sanaullah was the Model Town tragedy in 2014, where Punjab Police violently clashed with supporters of Tahir-ul-Qadri, resulting in multiple deaths. As the then-Law Minister, Sanaullah defended the police action, leading to public outrage and his temporary removal from the position. Though a joint investigation team later exonerated him, the incident remains unresolved.

In 2019, Sanaullah was arrested by the Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF) on charges of heroin trafficking, a case that carried severe penalties. He maintained his innocence, claiming the charges were politically motivated. After multiple legal battles, he was acquitted in December 2022. He alleged that the case was fabricated by political opponents, including figures from the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).

Sanaullah’s political journey has been marked by both successes and controversies, reflecting the complex nature of Pakistani politics. His legal and political acumen, combined with his enduring presence in the PML-N, have cemented his role as a key figure in the country’s governance.

title: Lokesh Kanagaraj
text:
Lokesh Kanagaraj, born on 14 March 1986 in Kinathukadavu, Coimbatore district, Tamil Nadu, is a prominent Indian film director, screenwriter, and producer known for his work in Tamil cinema. Hailing from a Tamil aristocratic family, he completed his schooling at Palanayiammal Matric Hr. Sec. School in Kalliyapuram, Pollachi, and later studied Fashion Technology at PSG College of Arts and Science before pursuing an MBA. Before entering the film industry, he worked as a bank employee. His passion for filmmaking began when he participated in a corporate short film competition judged by director Karthik Subbaraj, who was impressed by his work and encouraged him to pursue a career in filmmaking.

Lokesh’s directorial debut was the short film *Acham Thavir* (2012), which earned him awards for Best Director, Best Film, and Best Actor at the Clubace short film festival. In 2016, his short film *Kalam* was featured in the anthology film *Aviyal*, produced by Karthik Subbaraj. His first feature film, *Maanagaram* (2017), marked the beginning of his career in mainstream cinema. The turning point in his career came with *Kaithi* (2019), an action thriller starring Karthi, which was produced by Dream Warrior Pictures. The film’s commercial success led to the creation of the Lokesh Cinematic Universe (LCU), a franchise that connects his subsequent films through shared characters and narratives.

Following *Kaithi*, Lokesh directed *Master* (2021), a standalone film starring Vijay, which received positive reviews and became the highest-grossing Indian film of that year. He then directed *Vikram* (2022), the second installment in the LCU, featuring Kamal Haasan, Vijay Sethupathi, and Fahadh Faasil. This film further solidified his reputation in the industry. His next project, *Leo* (2023), became his most successful film, grossing over ₹600 crore worldwide and serving as the third installment in the LCU.

Beyond filmmaking, Lokesh has collaborated with Shruti Haasan on a musical project titled *Inimel*. He has also expanded his career into production, launching his own company, G Squad, in November 2023. His first production under this banner is *Fight Club*, directed by Vijay Kumar. Additionally, he announced a short film, *Chapter Zero*, as a prequel to *Kaithi 2*, set within the LCU. In April 2024, he revealed another production, *Benz*, directed by Bakkiyaraj Kannan and starring Raghava Lawrence, which was later confirmed to be part of the LCU in October 2024.

Lokesh announced in June 2023 that he plans to conclude his directorial career after completing 10 films. He has also been involved in Rajinikanth’s upcoming film, *Coolie* (formerly *Thalaivar 171*), produced by Sun Pictures and scored by Anirudh Ravichander.

Lokesh’s filmmaking style is primarily rooted in the neo-noir action genre, drawing inspiration from directors like John Woo, Martin Scorsese, and Quentin Tarantino. His films often feature retro songs, hyperlink narratives, and intense violence, though he has admitted to toning down such sequences to cater to family audiences. He avoids using ropes in stunt sequences to maintain a raw, brutal aesthetic. Despite criticisms of glorifying violence, he acknowledges his romanticization of it but strives to balance it with commercial appeal.

In his personal life, Lokesh married Aishwarya on 8 January 2012, and the couple has two daughters. He has a recurring creative team, including editor Philomin Raj, composer Anbariv (for five films), and music director Anirudh (for four films), among others.

Lokesh Kanagaraj’s contributions to Tamil cinema, particularly through the LCU, have established him as a significant force in the industry, known for his unique storytelling and stylistic choices.

title: Ted Mack (politician)
text:
Edward Carrington Mack (1933–2018) was an architect and politician who made history as the only person in Australia to be elected and re-elected as an independent to local, state, and federal government. Known as the "father of the independents," Mack was a staunch advocate for transparency, public participation, and financial responsibility in governance. He deliberately limited his political terms to avoid receiving a parliamentary pension, a principle he upheld throughout his career.

Born in Sydney’s Paddington suburb, Mack attended Sydney Boys High School and completed national service in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) from 1951 to 1952. He later studied architecture at the University of New South Wales, graduating in 1958. After marrying Wendy, he worked in London from 1958 to 1961 before returning to Australia, where he focused on designing hospitals and public housing. He played a key role in constructing the Port Kembla District Hospital and later became Architect-in-Charge of Hospital Design at the NSW Public Works Department. In 1972, he was appointed Assistant Chief Architect at the NSW Housing Commission, and from 1974 to 1980, he served as a part-time architecture tutor at UNSW. Additionally, in 1975, he joined a committee led by H.C. Coombs to advise on Aboriginal housing in remote areas.

Mack’s entry into politics began in 1974 when he was elected to the North Sydney Municipal Council after opposing a high-rise development near his home. Re-elected in 1977 and 1980, he served as mayor from 1980 to 1983 by aldermanic vote and again in 1983 and 1987 by popular vote. As mayor, he championed open government, ensuring all council meetings and files were accessible to the public. He reduced reliance on rates by diversifying council income, leading to a drop from 66% to 38% in the reliance on rates by 1987. Under his leadership, North Sydney Council undertook extensive public works, including parks, car parks, childcare facilities, and community centres, all without increasing rates. He famously sold the mayoral Mercedes-Benz to fund community buses and used his own 1951 Citroën as the mayoral car.

In 1981, Mack ran as an independent for the newly created state seat of North Shore, defeating Liberal opposition leader Bruce McDonald with Labor preferences. He was re-elected in 1984 and 1988 but retired abruptly in 1989, two days short of qualifying for a parliamentary pension, in protest against what he saw as political excesses. His retirement triggered three by-elections, all won by candidates he endorsed.

After a brief hiatus, Mack entered federal politics in 1990, winning the traditionally Liberal seat of North Sydney. He opposed unilateral tariff cuts, privatisation, and Australian involvement in the Gulf War, arguing that the conflict was driven by oil interests and geopolitical greed. He also opposed the appointment of an Indonesian general linked to East Timor’s occupation as Australia’s ambassador. In 1996, he retired again to avoid a pension, paving the way for Joe Hockey’s eventual victory in the seat.

Post-retirement, Mack became a prominent republican, serving on the 1999 referendum’s "no" campaign and advocating for an alternative republican model. In 1997, he was named one of Australia’s "National Living Treasures." In 2015, he supported independent candidate Stephen Ruff in the North Sydney by-election, criticising the Liberal Party’s pre-selection process.

Mack’s later years were marked by health struggles, including a terminal brain cancer diagnosis in 2016. He died in 2018 following a stroke, and in 2019, a park in North Sydney was renamed in his honour. His legacy as a reformer and principled independent remains influential in Australian politics.

title: Chris Duffield
text:
Christopher Paul Duffield, born on 20 May 1952, is a former senior public servant who held significant roles in local government, most notably as the Town Clerk and Chief Executive of the Corporation of the City of London. He was succeeded in this position by John Barradell in 2012. Duffield’s career in public service spanned nearly three decades, during which he worked in various capacities before joining the Corporation of London.

Duffield was raised as the son of Jack and Irene Duffield and received his early education at St Albans School, a private all-boys institution in Hertfordshire. He later attended Newcastle University, where he graduated in 1973 with a Bachelor of Arts (BA Hons). His professional career began in local government, where he gained experience in multiple roles before assuming senior positions. Before joining the Corporation of London, he served as the Chief Executive of Bexley Council. His career also included stints at the Greater London Council (GLC), Redbridge, and Essex, demonstrating his extensive background in public administration.

In September 2003, Duffield was appointed to the pivotal role of Town Clerk and Chief Executive of the Corporation of the City of London. This position came with a wide range of responsibilities, including overseeing the efficient management of City functions, acting as the primary advisor on policy and resources, and servicing meetings of the Court of Common Council and the Court of Aldermen, as well as their respective committees. Additionally, he was tasked with investigating complaints against the city, managing electoral registration, and overseeing public relations, economic development, and human resources. Beyond his role at the Corporation, Duffield also served as the Chief Executive of the Police Authority, where he was responsible for supervising all Police Authority staff and working closely with the chairman to ensure effective policing within the City of London.

Duffield’s professional affiliations include membership in the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA), a testament to his expertise in public finance and administration. His career reflects a deep commitment to public service, particularly in local governance and financial management.

On a personal level, Duffield is married and has three sons: Mark, Jack, and Joe Duffield. He is also a grandfather to four grandchildren: Amelia, Alex, Katie, and Stanley Duffield. His family includes a brother, Ian Duffield, who has two children, Paul and Melanie Duffield. This personal background highlights his connections beyond his professional life, showcasing a family-oriented side to his identity.

Duffield’s career exemplifies a long-standing dedication to public administration, marked by leadership in local government and key roles in the City of London. His contributions to policy, financial management, and governance were central to his professional legacy, leaving a lasting impact on the institutions he served.

title: Giorgi Papunashvili
text:
Giorgi Papunashvili, commonly known as Papu, is a Georgian professional footballer born on 2 September 1995. He plays as a winger and currently represents Azerbaijani club Zira. Papunashvili has also played for the Georgian national senior and youth teams throughout his career.

Papunashvili began his professional career at Dinamo Tbilisi, his hometown club. After spending a season with the reserve team, he was promoted to the first team in 2013 and made his debut in the Erovnuli Liga against Tskhinvali. During the 2014–15 season, he became a key player for Dinamo, scoring 16 goals in all competitions, including his first career hat-trick against Tskhinvali in October 2014. That season, Dinamo won the Georgian Cup, with Papunashvili contributing two goals in the final against Samtredia. He also helped the club win the Umaglesi Liga in 2013–14 and the Georgian Super Cup in 2014.

In 2015, Papunashvili signed a season-long loan deal with Werder Bremen, where he played for the reserve team in Germany's 3. Liga. However, his time there was marred by injury, as he missed 12 matches and only appeared in 20 games, scoring two goals.

In June 2017, he transferred to Spanish club Real Zaragoza, signing a four-year contract. He made his debut for Zaragoza in a match against Granada CF in August 2017. In January 2020, he joined Racing de Santander on loan until the end of the season.

Papunashvili's career has been marked by several short spells with different clubs. In December 2020, he moved to Cypriot club Apollon Limassol FC. In January 2022, he returned to Georgia to play for Torpedo Kutaisi. After six months, he transferred to Serbian side Radnički Niš. In 2023, he had brief stints with Samtredia and Telavi before joining Kapaz in the Azerbaijan Premier League. In August 2024, he signed a 1+1-year contract with Zira, another club in the Azerbaijan Premier League.

On the international stage, Papunashvili made his senior debut for Georgia in a 1–0 friendly loss against the United Arab Emirates in June 2014. He also represented Georgia's under-17 national team in the 2012 UEFA European Under-17 Championship in Slovenia, where he scored a memorable last-minute goal in a qualifying match against England.

Throughout his career, Papunashvili has been known for his attacking contributions, particularly during his time at Dinamo Tbilisi, where he was a standout player. Despite facing challenges, including injuries and frequent club changes, he has continued to play professionally in various leagues.

title: Nancy Onyango
text:
Nancy Asiko Onyango is a prominent Kenyan accountant, businesswoman, and corporate executive who currently serves as the Director of the Office of Internal Audit and Inspection at the International Monetary Fund (IMF). She assumed this role on February 1, 2018, following her appointment on December 4, 2017. Prior to this, she was the CEO of Reliance Risk Advisory Solutions, a consultancy firm based in Nairobi, Kenya.

Born in Kenya, Onyango began her formal education in local schools before pursuing higher education at the University of Nairobi (UoN). She earned a Bachelor of Commerce (BCom) degree in Accounting and Finance in 1987 and followed it up with a Master of Business Administration (MBA) in 1989. Later in her career, she furthered her education by enrolling in the United States International University Africa, graduating in 2016 with a Doctor of Business Administration (DrBA). During her doctoral studies, she also took courses at Columbia Business School in New York City.

Onyango’s professional career began with a significant stint at PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC). From July 1995 to December 1998, she worked as a manager at the firm’s London office in Uxbridge, United Kingdom. She was later promoted to senior manager, a position she held for three and a half years until August 2002. In 2005, she was appointed as a Partner at PwC, leading the consulting unit at PwC East Africa in Nairobi. Her focus was on technology, governance, risk, and compliance, a role she served in until June 2012. In 2012, she became the head of the newly established Risk Assurance Services Unit at PwC East Africa, a position she held until October 2014.

Following her tenure at PwC, Onyango joined Ernst & Young (EY) in January 2015 as a partner. She led the governance, risk, and compliance division for the African continent for 20 months, until August 2016. Her leadership in risk management and corporate governance was further recognized when she was appointed to lead the Internal Audit unit at the IMF, a role she began in February 2018.

In addition to her executive roles, Onyango holds several board positions. She serves as a non-executive director of the Kenya Commercial Bank Group and Cytonn Investments. She is also a board member of Fairtrade Africa, where she chairs the audit and finance committee. These roles reflect her extensive expertise in financial oversight and corporate governance.

Onyango is married and has three sons, balancing her professional achievements with family life. Her career has been marked by a steady progression in leadership roles across consulting and financial services, culminating in her high-profile position at the IMF, where she oversees internal audit and inspection, ensuring financial integrity and accountability within the organization. Her educational background, professional experience, and board memberships underscore her reputation as a distinguished figure in the fields of accounting and corporate governance.

title: Cobhams Asuquo
text:
Cobhams Asuquo, born on January 6, 1981, is a Nigerian musician, songwriter, and producer who began his career in the music industry after working as Head of Audio Productions at Questionmark Entertainment. In 2006, he established his own recording facility, and in 2008, he founded Cobhams Asuquo Music Productions (CAMP), which he co-managed with Bez Idakula and Stan Iyke. Asuquo has been instrumental in shaping the careers of numerous artists, including Asa, Banky W, Omawumi, and Tiwa Savage, among others. His production work spans across different genres, and he has collaborated with both local and international musicians, contributing to hits such as "Maintain in India," "Catch Cold," "Ego," and "Butterflies."

One of Asuquo’s most notable projects was producing Asa’s debut album, which included popular tracks like "Fire on the Mountain" and "Jailer." He has also worked extensively in film and stage, composing and arranging scores for productions like *A Voice for Ella*, *Sunshine*, and *Bent Arrows*. His contributions to music extend beyond Nigeria, as he has performed at international events such as the Harare International Festival of Arts, the French Cultural Center Concerts in Johannesburg and Paris, and the launch of MTV Base Africa in Abuja.

Asuquo’s influence in global music initiatives is evident through his participation in campaigns like the ONE Campaign, where he worked alongside artists such as D’banj, Femi Kuti, and Somi to raise awareness on agriculture in Nigeria. He was also involved in the UN Global Goals campaign, co-producing the song "Tell Everyone," which featured artists like Sauti Sol, Yemi Alade, and Diamond Platnumz. In 2014, he performed at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, and in 2015, he released his debut single, "Ordinary People," followed by other tracks like "Do the Right Thing," "Star of Wonder," and "Boosit" featuring Falz.

In addition to his production work, Asuquo launched a digital radio countdown show called *The Top 12 Countdown with Cobhams Asuquo*, which showcased emerging African and Nigerian music. He has also produced major events such as the Rhythm Unplugged show, Hennessy Artistry, and the first "One Africa" concert in Houston, Texas.

Asuquo is visually impaired, a fact that has not hindered his prolific career in music. He married Ojuolape Veronica Olukanni on December 2, 2010, and the couple has two sons. Despite his challenges, Asuquo has made significant contributions to African music, both as a producer and as an advocate for social and humanitarian causes.

title: Alexander Vovin
text:
Alexander Vladimirovich Vovin (1961–2022) was a prominent Russian-American linguist and philologist specializing in East Asian languages, particularly Japanese. Born in the Soviet Union, he earned his M.A. in structural and applied linguistics from Saint Petersburg State University in 1983, followed by a Ph.D. in historical Japanese linguistics and premodern Japanese literature in 1987, with a doctoral dissertation on the *Hamamatsu Chūnagon Monogatari* (ca. 1056). His early career began as a Junior Researcher at the St. Petersburg Institute of Oriental Studies (1987–1990) before he moved to the United States, where he held academic positions at the University of Michigan (1990–1994), Miami University (1994–1995), and the University of Hawaiʻi (1995–2014), rising to full professor in 2003. He also conducted research as a visiting professor at institutions in Japan, Germany, and France, including the International Research Center for Japanese Studies in Kyoto, Ruhr University Bochum, and the National Institute for Japanese Language and Linguistics (NINJAL) in Tokyo. In 2014, he became Director of Studies at the Centre de recherches linguistiques sur l'Asie orientale (CRLAO) at the School for Advanced Studies in the Social Sciences (EHESS) in Paris, a position he held until his death in 2022.

Vovin’s scholarly work focused on Japanese historical linguistics, with an emphasis on etymology, morphology, and phonology, particularly in the Nara period (710–792) and, to a lesser extent, the Heian period (792–1192). He was also deeply involved in the study of the Ainu language in northern Japan, as well as Inner Asian and Kra–Dai languages, often working with texts preserved only in Chinese transcription. His most ambitious project was a complete academic English translation of the *Man'yōshū* (ca. 759), the earliest and largest premodern Japanese poetic anthology, alongside a critical edition of the original text and commentaries. His final work, published in 2021, was on the *Bussokuseki no Uta* of Yakushi-ji temple in Nara. He was also coordinating the *Etymological Dictionary of the Japonic Languages* from 2019 until his death, though the project was terminated after his passing. A festschrift was dedicated to him in 2021 on his 60th birthday.

Vovin’s personal life included two marriages: first to Varvara G. Lebedeva-Vovina, with whom he had a son, Aleksei, born in 1982, and later to Sambi Ishisaki, a fellow Japanese language researcher, in 2000. They had two more children. He died on April 8, 2022, at the age of 61, from cancer.

Throughout his career, Vovin published extensively, contributing foundational works such as *A Reconstruction of Proto-Ainu* (1993), *Did the Xiongnu Speak a Yeniseian Language?* (2000), and *A Reference Grammar of Classical Japanese Prose* (2003). His *Descriptive and Comparative Grammar of Western Old Japanese* (published in two parts, 2005 and 2009) was particularly influential, as was his *Man'yōshū: A New English Translation* (2009–2018), which spanned 20 volumes. Other notable works include *Korea-Japonica: A Re-evaluation of a Common Genetic Origin* (2008) and *The Eastern Old Japanese Corpus and Dictionary* (2021, co-authored with Sambi Ishisaki-Vovin). His research often challenged conventional theories, such as his argument against the genetic relationship between Japonic languages and "Altaic" or Korean. His contributions to the field of historical linguistics were widely recognized, and his work remains a cornerstone for scholars studying East Asian languages.

title: Daniil Medvedev
text:
Daniil Sergeyevich Medvedev, born on 11 February 1996 in Moscow, is a Russian professional tennis player who has reached the top of the men’s singles rankings. He has won 20 ATP Tour singles titles, including the 2021 US Open and the 2020 ATP Finals. His breakthrough came in 2019, when he reached six consecutive tournament finals, including the US Open. In 2020, he won the ATP Finals, defeating the world’s top three players en route to the title. In 2021, he won his first major at the US Open, denying Novak Djokovic the Grand Slam. In 2022, he became the first man outside the Big Three (Djokovic, Nadal, Federer) to reach world No. 1 since Andy Roddick in 2004, the third Russian man to do so after Yevgeny Kafelnikov and Marat Safin.

Medvedev was introduced to tennis at age six when his mother saw an advertisement for lessons at his swimming pool. His first coach was Ekaterina Kryuchkova, who had also trained Vera Zvonareva. Before focusing on tennis, he studied physics and mathematics at a specialized school, later enrolling in economics at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations before dropping out. He later graduated from the Russian State University of Physical Education, Sport, Youth, and Tourism. His family moved to Antibes, France, where he trained at a tennis academy. His parents, Sergey and Olga, now live in France as retirees. Medvedev speaks Russian, French, and English fluently.
